title: What religion is
description: Britannica calls religion people's relation to what they regard as holy or sacred; worship, moral conduct, right belief and belonging to religious institutions make up religious life.

facts.text: Britannica defines religion as human beings' relation to that which they regard as holy, sacred, absolute, spiritual, divine, or worthy of especial reverence.
Worship, moral conduct, right belief and participation in religious institutions are among the constituent elements of religious life.

title: What nearly all religions share
description: Nearly every tradition has beliefs, practices, a community and sacred stories handed down.

facts.text: Ninian Smart wrote that it is typical of all faiths to hand down vital stories: about creation, great founders, saints and heroes, and things to come at the end of time.
Smart wrote that every religious movement is embodied in a group of people, very often formally organized, as a Church, Sangha or umma.

title: The world's major religious traditions
description: Christians and Muslims are the largest religious groups, then Hindus and Buddhists; Jews number about 15 million, and many smaller religions and the unaffiliated complete the picture.

facts.text: In 2020 Christians were the world's largest religious group, followed by Muslims, the religiously unaffiliated, Hindus and Buddhists; 75.8% of people identified with a religion.
Pew's 'other religions' category, 2.2% of the world in 2020, includes Baha'is, Daoists, Jains, Shintoists, Sikhs, Wiccans, Zoroastrians and many small groups.
About 14.8 million Jews, roughly 15 million, lived worldwide in 2020, about 0.2% of the world population.

title: Tylor: belief in spiritual beings
description: In 1871 Edward Tylor proposed a minimum definition of religion: belief in spiritual beings, a definition by content.

facts.text: In Primitive Culture (1871), the anthropologist Edward Burnett Tylor proposed a minimum definition of religion: 'the belief in spiritual beings'.

title: Durkheim: a moral community
description: In 1912 Emile Durkheim defined religion by what it does: beliefs and practices about sacred things that unite people into one moral community.

facts.text: In The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), Emile Durkheim defined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, 'set apart and forbidden', uniting its adherents into one moral community.

title: Why religion is hard to define
description: Scholars define religion either by content (belief in spiritual realities) or by function (what it does for people); each fits some traditions awkwardly.

facts.text: Substantive definitions of religion rest on belief in distinctive realities such as spirits; functional definitions rest on the role practices play in people's lives, such as creating social solidarity.
Buddhist teaching does not center on a creator God, yet scholars widely recognize Buddhism as a religion, a long-standing problem for definitions built on belief in gods.

title: 'Religion' as an imported word
description: In East Asia the concept of religion arrived with scholars about a century ago, and people there have long combined traditions rather than joining just one.

facts.text: The concept of religion was imported to East Asia by scholars only about a century ago, and translations such as Chinese zongjiao are often understood to mean organized, hierarchical religions.
In late imperial China, following one tradition did not involve a total commitment: a devoted Confucian scholar could take part in Daoist or Buddhist rituals.

title: Smart's seven dimensions
description: Ninian Smart described religions through seven dimensions: ritual, experience, narrative, doctrine, ethics, social institutions and material forms.

facts.text: In The World's Religions (1989), Ninian Smart described seven dimensions of religion: practical and ritual, experiential and emotional, narrative or mythic, doctrinal and philosophical, ethical and legal, social and institutional, and material.
In 1967 Ninian Smart became the founding professor of religious studies at Lancaster University.
Ninian Smart argued that the search for one essence common to all religions ends in vagueness, and that it is more practical to ask what a religion is.
Smart gave Passover as an example: as Jews share the meal, they retrace the story of the Exodus from Egypt, so ritual and story are bound together.
Smart wrote that experience and emotion feed the other dimensions: 'ritual without feeling is cold, doctrines without awe or compassion are dry'.
Smart's material dimension covers buildings, works of art and natural places held sacred, such as the river Ganges, the Jordan and Mount Fuji.

title: Describing a religion in balance
description: Smart's list exists so a description neglects neither ideas nor practices; it even fits secular worldviews like nationalism, which Smart did not call religions.

facts.text: Smart said the point of the seven dimensions is a balanced description of religions that neglects neither ideas nor practices.
Smart found many of the seven dimensions in nationalism, with anthems, flags and memorials, but held that secular worldviews should not really be called religions.

title: Bracketing: describing without judging
description: Scholars suspend judgment about a religion's truth (epoché, or bracketing) so they can describe it in its own terms, with empathy.

facts.text: Phenomenologists of religion use epoché, the 'bracketing' or suspension of judgment, to describe religions in their own terms from a standpoint empathetic with their adherents.

title: What scholars mean by 'myth'
description: In the study of religion, 'myth' means a sacred story and says nothing about whether it is true; to believers such stories are often history.

facts.text: Smart wrote that in the modern study of religion, calling a sacred story a myth carries no implication that it is false, and that to the believer such narratives are very often history.

title: No faith speaks with one voice
description: Every tradition is a loose family of subtraditions: Christian worship in a Baptist chapel and an Orthodox church can look very different.

facts.text: Smart contrasted a plain Baptist service in Georgia, with hymns, Bible-reading, prayers and preaching, and an Eastern Orthodox service in Romania, with candles, icons, processions and chanting.
Smart wrote that every religious tradition shows itself as a loosely held-together family of subtraditions.

title: The oldest burials
description: About 100,000 years ago at Qafzeh in Israel, people buried their dead with ochre and deer antlers: signs of ritual that may point to belief beyond death.

facts.text: Cuneiform, one of the earliest known writing systems, emerged in Mesopotamia near the end of the 4th millennium BCE, around 3200 BCE.
At Qafzeh cave in Israel, about 100,000 years ago, early modern humans buried their dead, with red ochre found near the bones suggesting it was used in a ritual.
The Qafzeh 11 burial, about 90,000 to 100,000 years old, held a youngster of about 12 to 13 with two deer antlers on the chest; researchers call it a deliberate, ceremonial burial.
The Smithsonian's Human Origins Program notes that early humans often buried the dead with beads and other symbolic objects, rituals that may imply a belief that identity extends beyond death.

title: Göbekli Tepe
description: Hunter-gatherers in southeastern Turkey raised carved stone pillars before farming began; scholars read the site as a ritual center, and newer digs show people lived there too.

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey was built in the 10th to 9th millennium BCE by hunter-gatherers who had not yet taken up farming.
Göbekli Tepe's T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons; some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions.
Excavator Klaus Schmidt saw Göbekli Tepe as a ritual center where no one lived; newer digs found hearths, houses and a rainwater cistern, so scholars now see a settlement with a religious center.

title: What makes a text scripture
description: A scripture is a text a community reveres as conveying sacred power or revelation; canons fix which texts count, by agreement or by religious authorities.

facts.text: Scriptures are revered texts believed to convey spiritual power or to be the means through which a divine being or other sacred reality is revealed.
The most sacred texts of a tradition are gathered into canons, fixed collections held fully authoritative, by general agreement or by official religious bodies.

title: Scripture kept by memory
description: Most scriptures began as oral traditions; the Vedas were kept word-perfect by trained recitation, and the Buddhist Pali canon was memorized for centuries before it was written down.

facts.text: Most sacred scriptures were originally oral and were passed down through memorization from generation to generation until they were committed to writing.
Most scholars accept about 1500 to 1200 BCE for the oldest Vedas, which Hindus regard as shruti, 'what is heard', and which were preserved orally.
To keep the sound of each word unaltered, Vedic reciters are taught from childhood complex recitation techniques based on tonal accents and exact pronunciation.
The Buddhist Pali canon was transmitted orally and first written down in Sri Lanka, probably in the 1st century BCE.
The word Quran means 'recitation', and verses from the Quran are recited during the five daily prayers.

title: Rites of passage
description: Ceremonies that move a person from one status to another, named by Arnold van Gennep in 1909 and found in every known society.

facts.text: The French anthropologist Arnold van Gennep introduced the term rite of passage in 1909 for ceremonies marking a move from one social or religious status to another, found in all known societies.
Rites of passage mark events such as birth, coming of age, marriage and death, and they teach new roles, reinforce social values and bring the community together.

title: Separation, transition, incorporation
description: Van Gennep's three stages: leaving an old status, an in-between threshold time (the liminal stage), and joining the community in a new status.

facts.text: Van Gennep found three stages in rites of passage: separation from an old status, transition (the liminal stage), and incorporation into the community with a new status.
The word liminal comes from Latin limen, 'threshold'.

title: Coming of age and the last rite
description: Jewish bar and bat mitzvah mark religious adulthood; Hindu antyeshti funeral rites carry the family through a set period of mourning.

facts.text: Bar and bat mitzvah mean 'son' and 'daughter of the commandment'; boys usually mark it at 13 and girls at 12 or 13, often with a first public Torah reading.
In the 20th century the bat mitzvah for girls spread widely across Conservative, Reform and some Orthodox congregations.
Hindu funeral rites, antyeshti, vary by caste and sect but generally involve cremation and placing the ashes in a sacred river.
For 10 days after a Hindu cremation the immediate family observe ritual restrictions and perform rites meant to help the soul of the dead on to its next life.

title: The Abrahamic family
description: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all revere Abraham; Jews and Christians trace the line through Isaac, Muslims through Ishmael.

facts.text: Judaism, Christianity and Islam, the Abrahamic religions, share reverence for Abraham, who is often considered the first monotheist.
Jews and Christians trace their story through Abraham's son Isaac, and Muslims through his son Ishmael.

title: The Indian family
description: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism began in the Indian subcontinent; karma, rebirth and release from rebirth run through this family.

facts.text: Karma, the law by which good or bad actions shape future existence, is generally shared among the religious traditions of India, with rebirth (samsara) and the goal of release (moksha).
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, which all began in the Indian subcontinent, are often grouped together as the Dharmic religions.
Sikhism was founded in the Punjab region of the Indian subcontinent in the late 15th century.

title: The East Asian family
description: Confucianism, Daoism, Shinto and Buddhism are often combined in East Asia, where honoring ancestors is widespread.

facts.text: Chinese religion draws on Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, often blended with folk traditions; Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan.
Britannica notes that East Asians may profess themselves Shintoists, Daoists, Buddhists, Muslims or Christians, but seldom cease to be Confucians.
In a 2023 Pew survey of East Asia and Vietnam, roughly half of adults or more in every place surveyed had offered food, water or drinks to their ancestors in the past year.

title: Indigenous traditions: many, not one
description: There is no single 'Native American religion': practices differ from people to people, are tied to particular places, and are passed on orally.

facts.text: Britannica stresses that there is no generic 'Native American religion': practices differ between peoples, are often localized to particular places, and are passed on orally.
The Menominee explain their origins through the geography of their own homeland.

title: How believers are counted
description: Researchers count religious groups from censuses and surveys that ask people their religion, so the numbers measure identity, not belief or practice.

facts.text: Pew's estimates of the world's religious groups in 2020 draw on more than 2,700 censuses and surveys, many asking a question like 'What is your religion, if any?'
In its global estimates, Pew counts Christians of all denominations as one group.
Since a 1976 law, the US census may not require anyone to answer questions about religious beliefs or membership, so private surveys supply the figures.

title: The world by religion, 2020
description: About 29% Christian, 26% Muslim, 24% unaffiliated, 15% Hindu and 4% Buddhist, with about 15 million Jews.

facts.text: In 2020 about 29% of the world's people were Christian, 26% Muslim, 24% religiously unaffiliated, 15% Hindu and 4% Buddhist.

title: What 'unaffiliated' means
description: The unaffiliated are people who call themselves atheist, agnostic or 'nothing in particular'; some still hold beliefs or keep practices.

facts.text: Pew's religiously unaffiliated are people who describe themselves as atheist, agnostic or 'nothing in particular', and some of them hold religious or spiritual beliefs and practices.
In Pew's 2023 survey, 92% of religiously unaffiliated adults in Vietnam said they had made an offering to ancestors in the past year.

title: How the study of religion grew
description: From Tylor (1871) and Durkheim (1912) to van der Leeuw (1933) and Smart (1967, 1989), scholars built tools to define and describe religions fairly.

facts.text: Gerardus van der Leeuw's classic 1933 text on the phenomenology of religion urged scholars to suspend their beliefs and describe religions in their own terms.

title: The covenant with Abraham
description: Jews believe God called Abraham from Ur and made a lasting covenant with him, promising the land of Canaan and many descendants.

facts.text: In Genesis (1917 JPS) God tells Abram: 'Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto the land that I will show thee.'
Abraham left Ur, in Mesopotamia, because God called him to found a new nation in a land he later learned was Canaan.
Abraham is best known for the depth of his faith; in Genesis he obeys the commands of God without question.
A covenant (Hebrew berit) is a binding agreement; in the Bible God binds himself by oath to fulfill promises to Abraham.
In Jewish tradition Abraham entered a covenant with God in which he was promised the land of Canaan and numerous descendants.
In Genesis 17 (1917 JPS) God renames Abram: 'thy name shall be Abraham; for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee.'
Genesis 17:7 (1917 JPS) calls it 'an everlasting covenant' between God and Abraham 'and thy seed after thee throughout their generations'.

title: Circumcision, the covenant's sign
description: Genesis 17 makes circumcision the covenant's sign; Jewish boys are circumcised on the eighth day in the rite of berit mila (brit milah).

facts.text: Genesis 17 (1917 JPS) makes circumcision of every male 'a token of a covenant', at eight days old.
A Jewish boy is circumcised on the eighth day after birth as a covenantal sign; the rite, berit mila (often spelled brit milah), includes blessings and naming.
In Judaism circumcision represents the fulfillment of the covenant between God and Abraham (Genesis 17).

title: Abraham's heirs in three faiths
description: Islam sees Ishmael as the fulfillment of the promise and Muhammad as his descendant; Christianity traces Jesus' genealogy to Isaac.

facts.text: In Islam the Prophet Muhammad is a descendant of Abraham's son Ishmael; in Christianity the genealogy of Jesus is traced to Isaac.

title: The Exodus as the Bible tells it
description: In the biblical account Moses led the enslaved Hebrews out of Egypt after the plagues and through the sea; Jewish tradition reveres him as the greatest prophet.

facts.text: In the biblical account a pharaoh enslaved the Hebrews in Egypt; after plagues he let them go, and Moses led them through the Red Sea, which God parted.
In the Jewish tradition Moses is revered as the greatest prophet and teacher.

title: The covenant at Sinai
description: At Sinai, the Bible tells, God made the Israelites his people and gave the terms of his covenant, beginning with a reminder of the Exodus; many Jews hold that an Oral Torah was revealed too.

facts.text: At Mount Sinai, in the biblical account, God made the Israelites his people and gave them the terms of his covenant, including the Ten Commandments.
The Ten Commandments open (1917 JPS): 'I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.'
Many Jews hold that the Oral Torah, laws and customs passed down by word of mouth, is part of God's revelation to Moses.

title: What historians can say about the Exodus
description: Archaeology has not confirmed the Exodus as the Bible describes it; Israel is first named outside the Bible by Merneptah about 1205 BCE; some historians see a smaller escape behind the story.

facts.text: The Bible scholar S. David Sperling notes that there is no archaeological evidence that the Israelites were ever in Egypt.
The earliest widely accepted mention of the name Israel is an inscription of the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah dating to about 1205 BCE.
Some historians argue that an escape from Egypt by some part of the later Israelite tribes lies behind the story, given its central place in Israel's faith.

title: The Tanakh and its parts
description: The Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh, has three parts (Torah, Neviim, Ketuvim) and 24 books; the Torah is its first five books.

facts.text: Tanakh is an acronym for the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible: Torah (Instruction, or Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).
The Hebrew canon contains 24 books, one for each of the scrolls on which they were written in ancient times.
Christians divided some of these books into parts, such as Samuel and Kings into two each and the Minor Prophets into 12, giving more books.
The Torah, the first division, includes the five books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.

title: The Torah scroll and its yearly reading
description: A handwritten Torah scroll is read aloud in the synagogue through the year; on Simchat Torah the reading ends and restarts at once.

facts.text: A Sefer Torah is the Torah written in Hebrew by a qualified scribe (sofer) on parchment, kept in the ark in synagogues.
The Torah scroll is read aloud at services on Sabbaths, Mondays, Thursdays and festivals, and taken out and returned with deep reverence.
On Simchat Torah the yearly cycle of Torah readings ends with the last part of Deuteronomy and restarts with the first part of Genesis.
On Simchat Torah people usually make seven circles around the reading platform carrying the Torah scrolls and dancing.

title: The First Temple and its fall
description: Solomon's Temple became Judah's only place of sacrifice; Babylon destroyed it in 586 BCE and deported many Judeans.

facts.text: The First Temple was completed under King Solomon in 957 BCE, in the 10th century BCE, and became the only place of sacrifice in Judah.
In 586 BCE the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and many Judeans were deported to Babylonia.

title: Faith in exile
description: In Babylonian exile Jews kept the Sabbath and circumcision and prayed in place of sacrifice; synagogues may have begun then.

facts.text: In exile in Babylonia, Jews kept the Sabbath and holidays, practiced circumcision and offered prayers in place of the Temple sacrifices.
Some scholars think synagogues first began during the Babylonian Exile, when homes were used for worship and instruction.
Psalm 137 (1917 JPS) begins: 'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.'

title: The Second Temple and what remains
description: Cyrus let exiles return in 538 BCE; the rebuilt Temple stood from about 515 BCE until Rome destroyed it in 70 CE. The Western Wall and Tisha b'Av keep its memory.

facts.text: In 538 BCE Cyrus the Great, the Persian conqueror of Babylonia, gave the Jews permission to return, though some chose to stay in Babylonia.
Work on the rebuilt Second Temple was completed in 515 BCE.
The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, during the Jewish rebellion against Rome.
The Western Wall is a surviving part of the retaining wall around the Temple Mount and a place of prayer sacred to Jews, where people push slips of paper with prayers into its cracks.
Tisha b'Av, on 9 Av (July or August), is a fast day of mourning for the destruction of the First and Second Temples, when Lamentations is read.

title: Johanan ben Zakkai and Yavneh
description: Johanan ben Zakkai founded an academy at Jabneh (Yavneh) and let Temple ceremonies be kept elsewhere, setting the terms for Judaism after the Temple.

facts.text: Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai's disciples are credited with smuggling him out of Jerusalem in a coffin, around 70 CE.
Johanan ben Zakkai set up an academy at Jamnia (Jabneh, or Yavneh), and so fixed the conditions for continuing Judaism after the Temple was destroyed.
He ruled that ceremonies once confined to the Temple could be kept outside it 'to serve as memorials of the Sanctuary'.

title: The synagogue and the minyan
description: After 70 CE the synagogue, a house of prayer, assembly and study with no sacrifice or priest, became the center of Jewish life; a minyan of ten can pray anywhere.

facts.text: The synagogue's Hebrew names call it a house of prayer, a house of assembly and a house of study.
After the Second Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, synagogues became the focal point of Jewish religious life; their worship has no sacrifice, so it needs no priesthood.
A minyan is the quorum of ten, traditionally men, needed for communal prayer; without one there is no public Torah reading. Reform and Conservative Judaism also count women.
In the Diaspora, the Jewish communities scattered outside the land, Jewish life centered on synagogues, the study of the Torah and prayer.

title: Rabbis, the Mishnah and the Talmud
description: Rabbis, interpreters of Jewish law, gathered the oral law into the Mishnah (early 3rd century CE); with the Gemara it forms the Talmud.

facts.text: Rabbi means 'my teacher' or 'my master'; by 100 CE the word meant a sage, an interpreter of Jewish law.
The Mishnah, the oldest authoritative collection and codification of Jewish oral law, was given final form early in the 3rd century CE by Judah ha-Nasi.
The Mishnah and the Gemara, a later commentary, together make up the Talmud, in which sages debate each text to exhaust its meaning.

title: Why Jews keep Shabbat
description: Shabbat, sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday, recalls God resting on the seventh day and is the only holiday in the Ten Commandments; Heschel called it a palace in time.

facts.text: Jews observe the Sabbath from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday; it is the only Jewish holiday mentioned in the Ten Commandments.
Genesis (1917 JPS) says God 'rested on the seventh day from all His work', and the commandment reads: 'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.'
In his 1951 book The Sabbath, Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel called the Sabbath 'a palace in time', a holiness found in time rather than in space.

title: How Shabbat is kept
description: Shabbat sets aside 39 categories of work (not when life is at risk), opens with candles, Kiddush and two challah loaves and closes with havdalah; observance varies.

facts.text: The Talmud lists 39 general categories of forbidden work on the Sabbath, including cooking and baking; they are set aside when life or health is seriously endangered.
Orthodox Jews strive to keep the Sabbath in full solemnity, while Conservative Jews vary in their practice, and so do Reform Jews, some of whom have held services on Sunday.
Before sunset on Friday, traditionally the woman of the house lights the Sabbath candles; the meal includes Kiddush, a blessing of sanctification over wine.
Two loaves of challah are served on Friday evening to commemorate the double portion of manna the Bible says God provided in the wilderness.
Havdalah ends the Sabbath with blessings over wine, spices and a braided candle, distinguishing the holy from the ordinary.

title: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
description: Rosh Hashanah opens the Ten Days of Repentance with the shofar; Yom Kippur, the holiest day, ends them with a 25-hour fast.

facts.text: Rosh Hashanah, the religious New Year on 1 Tishri (September or October), opens the Ten Days of Repentance, which end on Yom Kippur.
The shofar, a ram's horn, is sounded on Rosh Hashanah to call the Jewish people to a spiritual reawakening.
Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest and most solemn Jewish holiday, with a 25-hour fast and a day of prayer.
Before Yom Kippur friends ask each other's forgiveness, since obtaining forgiveness from one's fellows signifies God's forgiveness.

title: Sukkot and Passover
description: Sukkot recalls the wilderness years in huts; Passover retells the Exodus at the seder, with matzah and the four questions.

facts.text: Sukkot begins five days after Yom Kippur; families eat, and some sleep, in huts roofed with branches, recalling the Israelites' 40 years in the wilderness.
Passover, in March or April, commemorates liberation from slavery in Egypt; at the seder meal participants read the Exodus story from the Haggadah.
At the seder children ask four questions, beginning 'Why does this night differ from all other nights?'; matzah recalls dough that had no time to rise.

title: Hanukkah
description: Hanukkah ('dedication') recalls the Maccabees' rededication of the Second Temple in 164 BCE with eight nights of lights; it is traditionally a minor holiday.

facts.text: Hanukkah, meaning 'dedication', commemorates the Maccabees' rededication of the Second Temple in 164 BCE; one more candle is lit each night for eight days.
The Talmud tells of oil that burned for eight days; Hanukkah has traditionally been a minor holiday and is not mentioned in the Hebrew Bible.

title: The mitzvot
description: A mitzvah is a commandment of the Torah; the Talmud counts 613, rabbis added more, and good deeds count as mitzvot.

facts.text: A mitzvah is any commandment, law or statute in the Torah, and for that reason to be observed by all practicing Jews.
The Talmud counts 613 commandments in the Torah: 248 mandatory and 365 prohibitive.
Many more commandments were added over the ages by rabbinic leaders, such as lighting candles on certain festivals.
Jews consider all good deeds as fulfilling mitzvahs, because such actions express God's will.

title: Keeping kosher
description: Kosher food follows rules on permitted animals, a ritual slaughter and strict separation of meat and dairy; observant Jews keep them as divine command, and practice varies widely.

facts.text: Kosher means 'fit' or 'proper'; Jews who keep it eat only fish with fins and scales, certain birds, and mammals that chew the cud and have cloven feet.
The Torah (1917 JPS) permits 'the ox, the sheep, and the goat' and forbids the swine, which 'parteth the hoof... but cheweth not the cud'.
Kosher meat must come from animals slaughtered by a set ritual, and blood is removed by presoaking and salting.
The Torah says three times (1917 JPS): 'Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21).
Kashrut requires strict separation of meat and dairy, in eating and in preparation, with distinct sets of dishes and utensils.
For observant Jews no other motive for keeping kosher is required than that God has so ordained.
In Pew's 2020 survey of US Jews, 17% said they keep kosher at home, including 95% of Orthodox, 24% of Conservative and 5% of Reform Jews.

title: Orthodox, Conservative and Reform
description: The branches differ over how binding traditional Jewish law is: fixed for Orthodox, a living but sacred law for Conservative, a developing faith with ritual law optional for Reform.

facts.text: Orthodox Judaism holds that the Written Law and the Oral Law, codified in the Mishna and interpreted in the Talmud, are fixed and remain the sole norm of observance.
Orthodox Judaism keeps daily worship, kashrut, traditional prayers, intensive Torah study and separate seating for men and women in the synagogue.
Reform Judaism began early in the 19th century in Germany; the first Reform services, in 1810, used an organ, a choir and prayers in German.
Reform Judaism teaches that Judaism must be a living, constantly developing faith, and challenges the binding force of ritual laws and customs.
Conservative Judaism, inspired by Zacharias Frankel, treats the Law as sacred and a living force, and allows change less radically than Reform; it has ordained women rabbis since 1985.
In Pew's 2020 survey of US Jews, 37% identified as Reform, 17% as Conservative, 9% as Orthodox and about 4% with other branches; 32% named no branch.

title: Ashkenazi and Sephardi heritage
description: Ashkenazi and Sephardi name family heritage and custom (Central and Eastern Europe; Spain and Portugal), not branches of belief.

facts.text: Ashkenazim descend from Jews of the Rhineland and France who moved east to lands such as Poland and Lithuania; many spoke Yiddish.
Sephardim descend from the Jews who lived in Spain and Portugal, and many kept the Judeo-Spanish language, Ladino.
Sephardim differ from Ashkenazim in many ritual customs, but as a difference in traditional expression, not in sect; Jews of North Africa and the Middle East are more properly called Mizrahim.

title: The Talmud as Rabbinic Judaism's constitution
description: Completed about 600 CE, the Babylonian Talmud became the constitution and bylaws of Rabbinic Judaism.

facts.text: Completed about 600 CE, the Babylonian Talmud, the more authoritative of the two Talmuds, served as the constitution and bylaws of Rabbinic Judaism.

title: What historians accept about Jesus
description: Most historians accept that Jesus was a Jew from Nazareth in Galilee, baptized by John the Baptist, who preached the kingdom of God and was crucified in Jerusalem on Pontius Pilate's orders around 30 CE.

facts.text: The founder of what later became Christianity was not a Christian but a Jew, an itinerant prophet, teacher and healer in Galilee.
Most historians accept that Jesus was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, baptized by John the Baptist, and crucified in Jerusalem on the orders of Pontius Pilate.
Jesus was a Galilean from Nazareth, born about 6 to 4 BCE, who died about 30 CE in Jerusalem.
As a young adult, Jesus was baptized by the prophet John the Baptist.
The kingdom of God was central to Jesus's message, and he taught in parables.
Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect (governor) of Judaea from 26 to 36 CE, presided at the final trial of Jesus and ordered his crucifixion.

title: How historians know: Gospels and a Roman witness
description: The four Gospels are the main sources for Jesus, and the Roman historian Tacitus, no friend of Christians, independently recorded his execution under Pontius Pilate.

facts.text: The prime sources for knowledge of Jesus of Nazareth are the four canonical Gospels in the New Testament.

The Roman historian Tacitus wrote in his Annals that Christus, founder of the Christians' name, was put to death in Tiberius's reign by sentence of Pontius Pilate, and called the movement a pernicious superstition.

title: Christ: a title and a belief
description: Christ is a title, from Greek christos, the Messiah or 'anointed one'; Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead, and most regard him as God incarnate.

facts.text: Christ was not originally a name but a title, from the Greek christos, which translates the Hebrew meshiah (Messiah), 'the anointed one'.
Jesus's disciples became convinced that he rose from the dead and appeared to them; most Christians regard him as the Incarnation of God.

title: What the New Testament holds
description: The New Testament's 27 books (Gospels, Acts, letters, Revelation) were written in Koine Greek; Paul's letters are the oldest, and Christians place the collection after the Jewish scriptures, which they call the Old Testament.

facts.text: The New Testament has 27 books: the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the letters (Epistles) and Revelation.
Paul's letters, which address the immediate problems of local churches shortly after Jesus's death, are considered the earliest New Testament texts, though they come after the Gospels in its order.
Koine, the Greek used across Greece and Greek-ruled parts of Africa and the Middle East from the 4th century BCE to the mid-6th century CE, is the language of the New Testament.
The Christian Bible consists of the Old Testament, the Jewish scriptures as Christians read them, and the New Testament.

title: How the Gospels were written
description: For about 40 years after Jesus's death his story was retold aloud; Mark, around 70 CE, was the first Gospel, and the writers aimed to bear witness to a faith.

facts.text: Jesus died around 30 CE, and for about 40 years there was no written gospel: his followers passed on his story orally, telling and retelling it.
The word gospel comes from Anglo-Saxon god-spell, translating the Greek euangelion, 'good news'.
Most scholars agree that Mark was the first Gospel written, around 70 CE, weaving together earlier oral tradition; Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source.
The New Testament books were composed not to satisfy historical curiosity but to bear witness to a faith.

title: Settling the New Testament canon
description: Churches argued over which early writings counted; in 367 Athanasius of Alexandria listed exactly today's 27 books, more than three centuries after Jesus.

facts.text: The canon of 27 New Testament books appears for the first time in the 39th Festal Letter of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in 367 CE.
Athanasius wrote his list to end disputes over texts such as the Shepherd of Hermas, which some had long regarded as equal to the apostles' letters.

title: The Trinity
description: Christians believe in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons in one Godhead; the doctrine took its lasting form by the end of the 4th century.

facts.text: The Trinity is the Christian doctrine of the unity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three persons in one Godhead.
Neither the word Trinity nor the explicit doctrine appears in the New Testament; the doctrine took substantially its lasting form by the end of the 4th century.

title: The Nicene Creed
description: Against Arius, who taught that Christ was a created being, the Council of Nicaea in 325 called the Son homoousios, 'of one substance', with the Father; the creed churches use today was issued at Constantinople in 381.

facts.text: Arius taught that Christ was not divine but a created being; the Council of Nicaea in 325 condemned his teaching.
The Council of Nicaea declared the Son homoousios, Greek for 'of one substance', with the Father, to express their absolute equality.
The text now called the Nicene Creed was issued by the First Council of Constantinople in 381.

title: What a creed does
description: A creed is a brief, authoritative statement of a community's beliefs said in worship; the Nicene Creed is shared across Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and major Protestant churches, apart from the Western 'and the Son'.

facts.text: A creed is an authoritative formulation of a religious community's beliefs; creeds are brief affirmations used in worship.
The Nicene Creed is the only ecumenical creed, accepted as authoritative by the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican and major Protestant churches.
From the 6th century Western churches gradually added 'and the Son' (filioque) to the creed's words on the Holy Spirit; Eastern churches have always rejected it.

title: Baptism
description: Baptism with water is Christianity's rite of admission; most traditional churches baptize infants, while Baptists and others baptize only believers who profess their faith.

facts.text: Baptism is the Christian sacrament of admission: water, by immersion, pouring or sprinkling, with the words 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit'.
Paul described baptism as a personal sharing in the death, burial and Resurrection of Christ.

Most traditional churches, including Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed, baptize infants; Baptists and some others baptize only believers who profess faith, a practice rooted in the Anabaptists.

title: Communion (the Eucharist)
description: The Eucharist recalls Jesus's Last Supper with bread and wine; churches differ on what happens to them, from Catholic transubstantiation to a memorial meal.

facts.text: The Eucharist (Greek for 'thanksgiving'), also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, commemorates Jesus's Last Supper and is the central act of worship in most churches.
At the Last Supper, the Gospels say, Jesus blessed bread and wine and told his disciples to repeat the ceremony in his memory.
The Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation holds that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while keeping their appearance.

Orthodox churches affirm Christ's real presence in their own terms; Lutherans affirm a real presence but not transubstantiation; Zwingli saw a memorial; some churches call it an ordinance, not a sacrament.

title: The Christian year
description: The church year is built around Christ's life, death and resurrection: a Christmas cycle opened by Advent, and an Easter cycle from Lent through Easter to Pentecost.

facts.text: The church year is an annual cycle centered on Christ's life, death and resurrection: a Christmas cycle (Advent's four Sundays, Christmas, Epiphany) and an Easter cycle (Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost).
Christmas, the celebration of Jesus's birth, has a fixed date: December 25.
Easter celebrates the Resurrection of Jesus, on the third day after his Crucifixion.
Early Christians kept Sunday as 'the Lord's day' to commemorate the Resurrection, and the 50 days from Easter to Pentecost framed the first church year.

title: Lent
description: Lent is a 40-day season of penitence before Easter, recalling Jesus's fast in the wilderness, kept with fasting, prayer and giving.

facts.text: Lent is a 40-day season of penitential preparation for Easter, recalling Jesus's fast in the wilderness; Western churches begin it on Ash Wednesday, Orthodox Great Lent on Clean Monday.
Lent is kept with fasting, abstinence and almsgiving, and many Christians also give up pleasures such as sweets, alcohol or social media.

title: Why Easter moves
description: Easter is the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after March 21, so it falls between March 22 and April 25; Orthodox churches reckon it on the Julian calendar.

facts.text: Western churches keep Easter on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, fixed at March 21, so it falls between March 22 and April 25.
Eastern Orthodox churches calculate Easter by the Julian calendar, so their Easter usually falls later than the Western date.

title: How the Catholic Church is organized
description: The Catholic Church, the largest Christian church, is led by the pope as bishop of Rome and Peter's successor, with bishops over dioceses and parishes; cardinals elect a pope in a conclave.

facts.text: The Roman Catholic Church, with about 1.3 billion members, is the largest Christian church.
The pope is the bishop of Rome; the Catholic Church teaches that St. Peter was the first pope and regards each pope as his successor, with full authority over the whole church in faith and morals.
The Catholic Church traces an unbroken continuity from the apostles through its bishops, called apostolic succession.
A diocese is a territory administered by a bishop and divided into parishes; in the Catholic Church only the pope can create, divide or merge dioceses.
Cardinals under 80 elect a new pope in a conclave in the Sistine Chapel, by a two-thirds majority; burned ballots send up black smoke for no decision and white smoke for a new pope.

title: The seven sacraments
description: Catholics celebrate seven sacraments, visible signs of invisible grace; Protestant reformers generally kept only baptism and the Lord's Supper.

facts.text: The Catholic Church recognizes seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, reconciliation (penance), anointing of the sick, marriage and holy orders.
St. Augustine defined a sacrament as 'the visible form of an invisible grace'.
Protestant reformers generally accepted only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord's Supper.

title: The Orthodox family of churches
description: Eastern Orthodoxy is a communion of self-governing churches, with the Ecumenical Patriarch 'first among equals' rather than a pope; East and West separated in 1054.

facts.text: Eastern Orthodox Christians live mainly in the Balkans, the Middle East and former Soviet countries.

Eastern Orthodoxy is a communion of self-governing (autocephalous) churches, from the ancient patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem to the churches of Russia, Serbia, Romania and Greece.
The Patriarch of Constantinople, the Ecumenical Patriarch, is 'first among equals', with an honorary primacy but no papal authority over the other churches.
The schism of 1054 separated Eastern and Western Christianity, after disputes over papal claims to authority and the filioque.

title: Icons and the Divine Liturgy
description: Icons of Christ, Mary and the saints are central in Orthodox churches and homes; Orthodox teaching separates the honor given to icons from the worship owed to God alone.

facts.text: Icons, images of Christ, the Virgin Mary and the saints, hold a central place in Orthodox worship and in Orthodox homes.
Orthodox teaching distinguishes the veneration given to icons, honor that passes to the person depicted, from worship, which is due to God alone.
The Divine Liturgy is the heart of Orthodox worship; services are held in national languages, though some churches keep older liturgical languages.

title: Luther's protest of 1517
description: On October 31, 1517, Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses against indulgences to his archbishop; the door-posting story came later, printers spread his ideas within weeks, and he was excommunicated in 1521.

facts.text: On October 31, 1517, the German theologian Martin Luther challenged the church's practice of indulgences in his Ninety-five Theses, which he sent to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz.

The story of Luther posting the theses on the church door was first recorded nearly 30 years later by Philipp Melanchthon, who does not mention nails; Luther never mentioned it, and historians debate whether they were posted at all.
Luther's ideas were printed and reprinted within weeks of first circulating, and copies were read across Europe.
Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther on January 3, 1521; at the Diet of Worms that April, Luther refused to recant unless shown wrong by Scripture or reason.

title: Faith alone, scripture alone
description: Luther taught that salvation is God's gift received by faith, not earned by works (sola fide), and made scripture the final authority (sola scriptura), translating the Bible into German.

facts.text: Luther taught sola fide, that salvation is a gift God grants to sinners who have faith in Christ rather than something earned by good works, and sola scriptura, scripture as the final authority.
Luther translated the Bible into German, lessening lay people's dependence on church authority.

title: The Reformation's branches
description: The Reformation split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, with Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Anabaptist branches.

facts.text: The Reformation split Western Christianity and gave rise to Protestantism, with Lutheran, Reformed (Calvinist), Anglican and Anabaptist branches; Henry VIII founded the Church of England in 1534.

title: Christianity's shift south
description: In 1910 about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa held the largest share, driven by higher fertility in Africa and disaffiliation in Western Europe.

facts.text: In 1910 about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe; by 2010 only about a quarter (26%) did.
By 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as home to the most Christians: about 31% of the world's Christians, against 24% in Latin America and the Caribbean and 22% in Europe.
The shift was fueled by much higher fertility rates in Africa than in Europe and by widespread Christian disaffiliation in Western Europe.

title: Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity
description: Pentecostals, named for the Spirit's descent at Pentecost, seek baptism with the Holy Spirit; with charismatics they were about 27% of Christians in 2010, spread by lay leadership and evangelism.

facts.text: Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, when, as the Acts of the Apostles describes, the Holy Spirit descended on the first Christians in Jerusalem.
Pentecostals seek a post-conversion experience called baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually with speaking in tongues, and value gifts such as prophecy and healing.
In 2010 pentecostal and charismatic Christians together made up about 27% of all Christians.
Pentecostals believe God acts directly in everyday life through the Holy Spirit; they have long treated evangelism as every Christian's task and encouraged lay leadership.

title: Christianity's three great branches
description: In 2010 about half of Christians were Catholic, 37% Protestant and 12% Orthodox; they share the creed and core rites but differ over authority.

facts.text: In 2010 about half of the world's Christians were Catholic, 37% were Protestant (broadly defined) and 12% were Orthodox.

title: Muhammad and the first revelation
description: Muslims believe that in 610, in a cave on Mount Hira, the angel Gabriel ordered Muhammad to recite; Khadijah was the first to believe, and the revelations became the Quran.

facts.text: Muhammad was born about 570 in Mecca and died in 632 in Medina.
Muslims believe that in 610, as Muhammad meditated in a cave on Mount Hira, the angel Gabriel came to him and ordered him to recite.
Muhammad kept receiving revelations for the rest of his life; remembered and recorded, they form the text of the Quran.
Khadijah, a merchant who had employed Muhammad to manage a caravan to Syria and then married him, is often considered the first person to believe his message.
Khadijah reassured Muhammad of the authenticity of his first revelations.
The Arabic word islam literally means 'surrender'; a Muslim is one who accepts surrender to the will of God.

title: The hijra and the Islamic calendar
description: Muhammad preached that there is no god but God; opposed in Mecca, he led his followers to Medina in 622, the hijra, from which the Islamic calendar counts its years.

facts.text: Muhammad preached that there is no god but God and that life should be lived in submission to God's will; Mecca's powerful saw his popularity as a threat.
In 622 Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Yathrib, later called Medina; this hijra ('migration') is the year the Islamic calendar begins.

title: A human messenger, the last prophet
description: Muslims see Muhammad as the last of a line of prophets including Abraham, Moses and Jesus; the Quran presents him as human, and Muslims worship God alone.

facts.text: In Islam Muhammad is considered the last of a series of prophets that includes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Solomon and Jesus.
In the Quran Muhammad is presented as a human being with no divine qualities; in Islamic tradition he is God's messenger and the 'seal of the prophets'.

title: How the Quran is organized
description: The Quran has 114 suras divided into verses (ayat), ordered roughly from longest to shortest after a short opening sura, not in the order of revelation.

facts.text: The Quran is divided into 114 chapter-like units called suras, subdivided into verses called ayat, a word that literally means 'sign'.
Apart from the short opening sura, recited in each of the five daily prayers, the suras are ordered roughly by decreasing length.
The order of the suras does not follow the order in which they were revealed.

title: The Quran as God's word in Arabic
description: Muslims believe the Quran is God's speech revealed in Arabic, so they learn to recite it in Arabic and many treat a translation as an interpretation.

facts.text: Muslims traditionally believe the Quran, composed in an early form of Classical Arabic, is a literal transcript of God's speech.
Muslims believe the Quran was revealed to Muhammad in stages, in Arabic, over 23 years.
Muslims are taught to learn and recite the Quran in Arabic even when it is not their language; translations are not treated as the Quran in the ordinary sense.

title: Keeping the Quran by heart and by voice
description: Muslims believe the standard text was set under the caliph Uthman; memorizers (hafiz) and skilled reciters, women and men, keep it alive by voice.

facts.text: Muslims believe the standard text of the Quran was established shortly after the Prophet's death by the caliph Uthman.
Learning the Quran by heart helped preserve it; a person who has memorized the whole Quran is known as a hafiz.
Quran recitation is a refined art, shown at popular competitions where renowned reciters, both male and female, display skills mastered over years.

title: Tawhid: the oneness of God
description: Tawhid, 'asserting oneness', holds that God is one and has no partners; shirk, associating anything with God, is its opposite. Allah is the Arabic word for God.

facts.text: Tawhid, literally 'making one' or 'asserting oneness', is the Islamic teaching that God is one: a unity, not made up of parts.
Tawhid is expressed in the shahada, the testimony 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is his messenger.'
Muslims believe God has no children, no parents and no partners, and has no shape or form that can be seen.
In Muslim teaching the one sin God will not forgive in the hereafter is shirk, associating others with God.
Allah is the standard Arabic word for God, probably a contraction of al-Ilah, 'the God', and is used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as Muslims.

title: The six articles of faith
description: Muslims hold six main beliefs: God, angels, revealed books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and God's decree; surveys show they are widely but not uniformly held.

facts.text: Muslims hold six main articles of faith: belief in God, in angels, in the holy books, in the prophets, in the Day of Judgement and in predestination.
Among Muslims' core beliefs is that God's angels exist even if people cannot see them.
Muslims believe God knows all that will happen, and that this does not stop human beings from making free choices.

In Pew surveys in 39 countries, belief in one God and in Muhammad as his Prophet was nearly unanimous in most; belief in fate ranged from under half in Albania to over nine in ten in Azerbaijan and Turkey.

title: The Five Pillars of Islam
description: The shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj are Islam's five pillars; together they give a Muslim's life its framework, and sincerely reciting the shahada makes a person a Muslim.

facts.text: The Five Pillars of Islam are the shahada (profession of faith), salat (prayer five times a day), zakat (alms for the poor), sawm (fasting in Ramadan) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).
Carrying out the Five Pillars gives a Muslim's life its framework, weaving everyday activities and beliefs into one cloth of devotion; Islam regards faith without practice as pointless.
Sincerely reciting the shahada is all a person needs to do to become a Muslim.

title: A day, a year, a lifetime
description: Prayer returns five times a day, zakat and the Ramadan fast once a year, the hajj once in a lifetime for those able; zakat is 2.5 percent of savings above a threshold, given as worship.

facts.text: Zakat is the yearly giving of 2.5 percent of one's wealth, such as cash and savings above a minimum threshold, to benefit the poor.
Muslims regard zakat as a form of worship and self-purification, and a reminder that wealth is held on loan from God.
Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the hajj to Mecca at least once in a lifetime.

title: How salat is performed
description: Muslims pray at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and evening, after ablution, facing the Kaaba in Mecca, through units of standing, bowing and prostration.

facts.text: The five daily prayers are fajr (dawn), zuhr (midday), asr (afternoon), maghrib (sunset) and isha (evening).
The muezzin chants the call to prayer aloud from a raised place, such as a tower, in the mosque.
Before prayer Muslims perform ablution (wudu), washing the hands, face and feet; mosques have washing facilities.
Muslims pray facing the Kaaba, a cube-shaped shrine near the center of the Great Mosque in Mecca; this direction is the qibla.
In a mosque, a niche called the mihrab points to the qibla, the direction of Mecca.
Each unit of prayer (rakah) includes standing, a bow and two prostrations, and 'God is great' is said at every change of posture.

title: Praying together and Friday prayer
description: Muslims pray directly to God and can pray anywhere; praying together shows equality, and on Friday the midday prayer becomes a congregational prayer with sermons.

facts.text: In prayer each Muslim is in direct contact with God, with no priest as an intermediary; the imam who leads mosque prayer is not a priest.
Muslims can pray anywhere, but praying with others in a mosque is especially valued as a sign that all are equal before God.
On Fridays, instead of the prayer just after noon, Muslims offer a congregational prayer (jumu'ah) that includes two sermons from the pulpit.

title: The Ramadan fast
description: In Ramadan, the ninth month, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset to grow mindful of God, with exemptions for those who cannot; Muslims believe the Quran's revelation began in this month.

facts.text: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar; Muslims fast from dawn until sunset, abstaining from food, drink and sexual activity.
Pregnant or nursing women, children, the old, the ill, the disabled and travelers on long journeys are exempt from fasting.
Muslims eat a meal called suhur before dawn; the iftar after sunset usually begins with dates, as was Muhammad's custom.
The Quran says fasting is prescribed so that believers may become mindful of God; Muslims also see it as learning self-discipline and sharing the sufferings of the poor.
The fast also means avoiding immoral behavior; false words or bad deeds are deemed as destructive of a fast as eating or drinking.
Muslims believe God's revelation of the Quran to Muhammad began on one of the last ten nights of Ramadan in 610, remembered as Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power.

title: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha
description: Eid al-Fitr ends the Ramadan fast; Eid al-Adha, at the height of the hajj, remembers Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son, with meat shared among family, friends and the poor.

facts.text: Eid al-Fitr, the 'Feast of Fast-Breaking' and one of the two major holidays of the Muslim calendar, celebrates the end of Ramadan: children wear new clothes, gifts are exchanged, and people gather for family meals and prayers in mosques.
At Eid al-Fitr Muslims thank God for the strength to practise self-control through Ramadan.

Eid al-Adha, the 'Festival of Sacrifice', begins on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah at the culmination of the hajj and commemorates Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son Ishmael, who was replaced by a ram.
At Eid al-Adha families pray together, sacrifice an animal and divide the meat among the poor, relatives, friends and their own household.

title: The rites of the hajj
description: From the 7th to the 12th of Dhu al-Hijjah pilgrims circle the Kaaba, walk between Safa and Marwa, stand at Arafat, stone the pillars at Mina and sacrifice an animal.

facts.text: The hajj begins on the 7th day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic year, and ends on the 12th.
Pilgrims walk around the Kaaba counterclockwise seven times.
Pilgrims walk seven times between the small hills of Safa and Marwa; Muslims believe Hagar ran between them seeking water for her son Ishmael before the spring of Zamzam gushed from the ground.
Pilgrims stand praising God in the open on the plain of Arafat, spend the night at Muzdalifah, then throw stones at pillars at Mina that represent the devil.
Pilgrims sacrifice an animal in memory of Abraham's sacrifice; men usually shave their heads and women remove a lock of hair.

title: Ihram: dressed as equals
description: Pilgrims enter ihram, a state of ritual purity with simple clothing, which strips away markers of wealth and status so that all stand equal before God.

facts.text: Pilgrims enter ihram, a state of ritual purity; men wear two white seamless sheets wrapped around the body, while women may wear sewn clothes.
The hajj is meant to show that everyone is equal before God: simple white ihram clothes strip away all markers of social status, wealth and pride.

title: The succession question
description: After Muhammad died in 632, the larger group chose Abu Bakr as caliph (Sunnis), while others held that Ali and his descendants should lead (Shia); Husayn's death at Karbala in 680 is central to Shia memory.

facts.text: Sunni and Shia identities first formed around a dispute over who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad's death in 632.
The larger group of Muslims chose Abu Bakr, a close Companion of the Prophet, as caliph; Sunnis recognize the first four caliphs as Muhammad's rightful successors.
Shia Muslims hold that leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants; the name Shia comes from 'Shiat Ali', the partisans of Ali.
Sunni means one who follows the Sunnah, what the Prophet said and did.
Ali became the fourth caliph and was killed in 661; in October 680 his son Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with most of his companions at Karbala.
Shia Muslims mourn Husayn each year at Ashura; Twelver Shia recognize twelve Imams in Ali's line, the last believed hidden until he returns as the Mahdi.

title: Two branches, one faith
description: Sunnis and Shia share the Quran and Islam's fundamentals and agree Muhammad was the final prophet; about 87 to 90 percent of Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 13 percent Shia.

facts.text: Sunnis and Shia agree on the fundamentals of Islam, share the same holy book, the Quran, and both hold that Muhammad was the final prophet.
In 2009 Pew estimated that 87 to 90 percent of the world's Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 13 percent are Shia.
Shia Muslims make up a majority of the population in four countries: Iran, Azerbaijan, Bahrain and Iraq.

title: Hadith and the Sunnah
description: Hadith report what Muhammad said and did; checked through chains of narrators and gathered into collections such as al-Bukhari's, they are a source second only to the Quran.

facts.text: Hadith are the reported sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad, revered by Muslims as a source of religious law and moral guidance second only to the Quran.
Sunnah, 'established custom', refers to the norms and practices affirmed or instituted by Muhammad.
Each hadith carries a chain of narrators (isnad) back to Muhammad and his Companions, plus its text (matn); scholars graded reports as sound, fair or weak.
Al-Bukhari (died 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (died 875) each compiled a collection titled 'The Authentic'; both are among the six canonical Sunni collections.
Shia Muslims have their own authoritative hadith collections, such as al-Kulayni's Kitab al-kafi.
After Muhammad's death his wife Aisha spent her years transmitting hadith and interpreting the Quran; traditional sources describe her issuing legal opinions.

title: From sharia to rulings: fiqh and the schools
description: Sharia is the path Muslims believe God set; fiqh is the human effort to know it, using the Quran, Sunnah, consensus and analogy, and four Sunni schools reach different rulings by different methods.

facts.text: Sharia literally means 'path leading to the watering place'; fiqh, literally 'understanding', is the jurisprudence that works out its precise terms.
Sharia is considered divine and unchanging, while fiqh, the human effort to know it, is imperfect and changeable.
The main sources of sharia are the Quran, the Sunnah, ijma (the consensus of scholars) and qiyas (reasoning by analogy).
Through qiyas, jurists ruled drugs forbidden by analogy with the Quran's ban on alcohol, because both share the cause of intoxication.
Sunnis accept four schools of Islamic law as orthodox: Hanafi, Hanbali, Maliki and Shafii.
The schools differed in method: the Malikis and Hanafis gave greater weight to their regional traditions, while al-Shafii emphasized the Quran and Sunnah and systematic analogy.
Hanafi law came to predominate in the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent, Maliki law in North, West and Central Africa, and Hanbali law in Saudi Arabia.
A saying attributed to the Prophet holds: 'Difference of opinion among my community is a sign of God's bounty.'

title: How belief, practice and law fit together in Islam
description: Tawhid is voiced in the shahada, the first pillar; the pillars shape time; and law grows from the Quran and hadith, which serve law, ritual and creed alike.

facts.text: Hadith are an important source, second only to the Quran, for Islamic law, ritual and creed alike.

title: Hinduism as a family of traditions
description: Hinduism has no single founder, scripture or agreed set of teachings; most Hindus share the Veda and dharma, and most live in India.

facts.text: Hinduism has no single founder, no single scripture and no commonly agreed set of teachings; over its long history many teachers taught different philosophies and wrote many holy books, so writers often call it 'a way of life' or 'a family of religions'.
Although Hinduism is hard to define, it is rooted in India, most Hindus revere a body of scripture called the Veda, and most draw on a shared system of values called dharma.
In 2020 India was home to 95% of the world's Hindus.

title: Where the word 'Hindu' comes from
description: 'Hindu' comes from Sindhu, the river Indus, used by Persians and Greeks for the land's people; 'Hinduism' was coined in the 19th century; many Hindus call their tradition sanatana dharma.

facts.text: The term Hindu comes from Sindhu, the Sanskrit name of the river Indus; Persians and later Greeks used the river's name for the land and its people.
The word 'Hinduism' was coined by British writers in the early 19th century.
Many Hindus prefer to call their tradition sanatana dharma, 'eternal law' or 'eternal order', a name popularized in the 19th century.

title: The four Vedas and their layers
description: Four Vedic collections, each with Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads; the Upanishads come last and are called Vedanta.

facts.text: The Yajurveda served priests as a handbook for performing Vedic sacrifices, and the Samaveda holds chants and tunes sung at the sacrifices.

There are four Vedic collections, the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda, each with four layers: Samhitas, largely hymns praising gods; Brahmanas, mostly explaining rituals; Aranyakas; and Upanishads.
The oldest Upanishads, such as the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, are generally dated between 700 and 500 BCE; some of their sections turn to inquiry about life, death and the nature of reality.
Vedanta means 'end of the Vedas' and is often used to refer specifically to the Upanishads.

title: Atman and Brahman in the Upanishads
description: Uddalaka's salt lesson and 'you are that'; atman is the eternal self, Brahman the power upholding everything; some teachers and later Shankara identify them.

facts.text: In the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water; the next day he cannot see it but tastes it throughout, and Uddalaka says the self is likewise unseen yet present throughout.
Uddalaka repeatedly tells his son 'you are that' (tat tvam asi); the philosopher Shankara later read it as saying the self (atman) is identical with Brahman.
Atman means 'eternal self'; Brahman is a transcendent power that upholds and supports everything.
Some Upanishadic teachers, such as Yajnavalkya, equate atman with Brahman, while Uddalaka never uses the word brahman.

title: Karma and samsara
description: Karma means action and its results across lifetimes; samsara is the cycle of rebirth of an eternal self through many bodies.

facts.text: Karma literally means 'action': good actions, in harmony with dharma, bring good results and bad actions bad ones, in this life or in a future life.
Samsara is the continuous cycle in which the soul is reborn again and again according to the law of action and reaction; many Hindus believe the soul may pass into a human, animal or divine body.
Because the self (atman) is understood as eternal, the same being can inhabit a series of temporary bodies.
Hindus believe the results of actions may come in this life, in a future human rebirth, or in a heavenly or hell realm where the self is reborn for a period of time.

title: Moksha, the final aim
description: Moksha, release from the cycle of rebirth, was added to three goals of life and is treated as the final and ultimate aim.

facts.text: Moksha, liberation, frees the self from the cycle of action and reaction and from rebirth.
Hindu texts name three goals of life, virtue (dharma), worldly success and pleasure; a fourth goal, liberation (moksha), was added later.
Moksha is the final of the four traditional aims of life, and the Brahma Sutra, the oldest systematic reading of the Upanishads, holds it to be the ultimate goal.

title: One divine, many forms
description: Most Hindus believe in one Supreme God whose forms are many deities; each person may choose a form (ishta devata).

facts.text: Most Hindus believe in a Supreme God whose qualities and forms are represented by many deities; many believe all the deities are aspects of a single transcendent power, and some see particular deities as manifestations of Brahman.
Outsiders often call Hindus polytheistic, but many Hindus describe themselves as monotheists.
Each person can relate to God through a particular chosen form, the ishta devata or 'desired form of God': one may be drawn to Shiva, another to Krishna, another to Kali.

title: Vaishnavism, Shaivism and Shaktism
description: Three great devotional traditions centered on Vishnu, Shiva and Devi; the Trimurti of creator, preserver and destroyer.

facts.text: In the Gupta period (320 to 500 CE) the great traditions of Vaishnavism, focused on Vishnu, Shaivism, focused on Shiva, and Shaktism, focused on Devi, the Goddess, developed.
Vaishnavism, devotion to Vishnu and his avatars such as Rama and Krishna, is one of the major forms of modern Hinduism.
In the Trimurti, Brahma is the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer, who destroys in order to re-create.

title: The Bhagavad Gita's setting
description: A dialogue in the Mahabharata's sixth book between Prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer, as Arjuna hesitates to fight; classed as smriti, yet one of the most popular Hindu texts.

facts.text: The Bhagavad Gita is part of the sixth book of the Mahabharata (chapters 23 to 40 of Book VI).
The Gita is a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and Krishna, his charioteer, as Arjuna wants to withdraw from a war that means killing relatives, friends and teachers.
The Bhagavad Gita, 'Song of the Lord', is smriti, 'remembered' tradition, rather than shruti like the Vedas, yet it is one of the most popular Hindu texts.

title: The Gita's three paths
description: Action without attachment to results (karma), knowledge (jnana) and devotion (bhakti) as paths to liberation.

facts.text: Krishna teaches Arjuna the path of action: do one's duty but act without desire (nishkama karma), giving up attachment to the results.
In the Gita, Krishna presents paths of action (karma), knowledge (jnana) and devotion (bhakti), with devotion presented as resolving the tension between action and knowledge.
Britannica describes three paths to liberation in Hinduism: the way of action or ritual duty (karma-marga), of knowledge (jnana-marga) and of devotion (bhakti-marga).

title: Puja, Hindu worship
description: Ceremonial worship from brief home rites to temple rituals: offerings, blessed food, and daily care of the sacred image.

facts.text: Puja is Hindu ceremonial worship, ranging from brief daily rites in the home to elaborate temple rituals.

Most Hindu homes have a shrine, which may be a room, a small altar or simply pictures, where offerings of water, fruit, flowers and incense are made; puja is mainly an individual act, not a communal one.

Puja includes seeing the deity, offerings such as flowers, fruits and food, and receiving the blessed food; in temples, priests perform puja at sunrise, noon, sunset and midnight, and images may be bathed and clothed.

title: Darshan: seeing and being seen
description: Beholding a deity's image, a revered person or a sacred object, a two-way blessing that also drives pilgrimage.

facts.text: Darshan is the beholding of a deity, especially in image form, a revered person or a sacred object; it works both ways, and the viewer is blessed by being seen.
For Hindus, pilgrimage is an undertaking to see and be seen by the deity; rivers are popular destinations, along with temples and mountains.

title: Diwali, the festival of lights
description: A five-day festival of lamps at the new moon of Kartika, with different stories across India and among Jains and Sikhs.

facts.text: Diwali, from Sanskrit dipavali, 'row of lights', is a five-day festival at the new moon of the month Kartika, usually in October or November.

At Diwali, homes are lit with diyas, small earthenware oil lamps, to honor Lakshmi, goddess of wealth; in northern India many recall Rama's return to Ayodhya, in the south Krishna's victory over Narakasura.
Diwali celebrates the victory of good over evil and light over darkness, though its legends differ in different parts of India.
Jains mark Diwali as the liberation of Mahavira, the most recent Tirthankara, and Sikhs as Guru Hargobind's return to Amritsar from captivity.

title: Holi, the festival of colors
description: A spring festival at the full moon of Phalguna with bonfires recalling Prahlada and Holika, colored powder, and social rankings set aside.

facts.text: Holi falls on the full moon of Phalguna, in February or March; people throw colored powders and colored water on one another and light bonfires.
Holi's bonfires recall Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, who survived when his aunt Holika, protected against fire, burned instead: a story of good over evil.
During Holi, participants set aside usual social norms and rankings before order is restored.

title: Why Hindu festival dates move
description: Hindu festivals follow lunar months in a lunisolar calendar, so their Gregorian dates shift each year.

facts.text: The Hindu calendar counts 12 lunar months, about 354 days, adjusted by adding extra months, so festival dates shift from year to year against the Gregorian calendar.

title: Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara
description: Jains believe their teachings are eternal; Mahavira, a prince turned ascetic and contemporary of the Buddha, is the 24th and last Tirthankara of this age.

facts.text: Jain tradition tells that Mahavira was born Vardhamana, a prince, left the palace at 30, and spent twelve and a half years fasting and meditating before reaching enlightenment.
Mahavira's traditional dates are 599 to 527 BCE, though some modern scholars place his birth around 540 BCE or later; he was a contemporary of the Buddha.
Digambara and Svetambara Jains agree on the basics but disagree on details of Mahavira's life, on whether monks should wear clothes, and on which texts are scripture.
Jains believe their teachings are eternal and have no founder; Mahavira, 'Great Hero', is the 24th and last Jina, or tirthankara, of the current cosmic period.
A tirthankara, 'ford builder', is one who shows others how to cross the currents of life by shedding desire and freeing the self from ignorance.
Jina means 'conqueror', one who has conquered the passions to gain enlightenment; Jains are followers of the Jinas.

title: Ahimsa toward every living thing
description: Jains believe every living thing has a soul and that harm binds karma, a physical substance, to one's own soul, so non-violence is central.

facts.text: Jains believe every living thing has a soul (jiva); earth, water, fire, air and plant beings have one sense, touch, and insects such as ants have three.
Jains believe karma is a physical substance that sticks to the soul through its actions, words and thoughts, and that harming others attracts much karma.
Ahimsa, non-violence, is the most central Jain teaching: Jains believe the only way to save one's own soul is to protect every other soul.

title: The five Jain vows
description: Non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint and non-possession, kept fully by monks and nuns and in a lesser form by laypeople.

facts.text: The five Jain vows are non-violence (ahimsa), truthfulness (satya), not stealing, sexual restraint, and non-attachment to possessions (aparigraha).
Monks and nuns keep the five vows as mahavratas, 'great vows'; laypeople keep them as anuvratas, 'lesser vows'.

Lay Jains keep the vows in a limited way, since full non-violence is not compatible with everyday life: they are vegetarian, filter drinking water, avoid eating at night and possess only what they need.

Jain monks sweep the ground with great care to avoid crushing insects, and some wear cloths over their mouths; Digambara monks own only a whisk broom for sweeping insects from their path and a water pot.
Jains have two major sects: Digambara, 'sky clad', whose monks wear no clothes, and Svetambara, 'white clad', whose monks and nuns wear white.

title: Many-sided truth (anekanta)
description: No single view captures the whole truth, as the parable of the blind men and the elephant shows.

facts.text: Anekanta, 'non-one-sidedness', holds that no single view or statement captures the complete truth about what it describes.
In the Jain parable of the blind men and the elephant, each touches one part: the ear seems a fan, a leg a post, the side a wall.

title: One life and a final judgment
description: Traditional Judaism, Christianity and Islam look to the end of history, resurrection and a Last Judgment after one lifetime.

facts.text: Eschatology first referred to Jewish, Christian and Muslim beliefs about the end of history, the resurrection of the dead and the Last Judgment.
Reincarnation is not an approved doctrine of orthodox Christianity, Islam or Judaism, which hold to one lifetime, one Day of Judgment and resurrection.
Muslims believe in a Day of Judgement, when the life of every human being will be assessed to decide whether they go to heaven or hell.
The Catholic Church teaches, with the creeds, that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead.
Maimonides counted resurrection of the dead among his 13 principles of Jewish faith, though the doctrine has been debated throughout Jewish history.

title: Time as a line or a cycle
description: Biblical eschatology looks to a historical future; many other religions see cycles of cosmic destruction and rebirth.

facts.text: Biblical eschatologies are directed toward a historical future, while in many religions outside the biblical tradition there is no 'end' but a cycle of cosmic destruction and rebirth.

title: The Buddha's traditional story
description: Buddhist tradition tells how Siddhartha Gautama, born at Lumbini, left a life of luxury at 29 after the Four Signs, practiced austerities for six years and awakened at Bodh Gaya, then taught for 45 years.

facts.text: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini, in what is now southern Nepal, into the Shakya clan; he is often called Shakyamuni, "sage of the Shakyas".
Traditional accounts say that at 29, after seeing an old man, a sick person, a corpse and a monk, Prince Siddhartha left his life of luxury.
After leaving home he lived as an ascetic, practicing renunciation and self-denial, for six years.
Buddhists hold that he attained enlightenment under a pipal tree, the Bo tree, at Bodh Gaya in Bihar, northeastern India.
Buddha means an awakened one: one who has awakened from the sleep of ignorance and been freed from suffering.
Tradition says the Buddha spent 45 years teaching across northeastern India and died at Kusinara (Kushinagar) at about 80.

title: What historians can say about the Buddha
description: Scholars accept that the Buddha lived, but the stories of his life cannot be taken with confidence as history; his death is dated around 480 BCE or up to a century later, and full biographies came centuries afterward.

facts.text: Scholars accept the Buddha's historical existence, but the events set out in the texts about his life cannot be regarded with confidence as historical.
20th-century scholars placed the Buddha's death around 480 BCE or as much as a century later.
An inscription recording the visit of Ashoka, Maurya emperor from about 273 to 232 BCE, to the spot he considered the Buddha's birthplace shows the Lumbini tradition existed by the 3rd century BCE.
Biographies of the Buddha began to be composed only around the beginning of the Common Era, centuries after his death.

title: The first sermon at Sarnath
description: After his enlightenment the Buddha taught five ascetics, his former companions, at the Deer Park in Sarnath, which Buddhists call setting the wheel of the dharma in motion.
