facts.text: After his enlightenment the Buddha gave his first sermon to five ascetics, his former companions, at the Deer Park in Sarnath; Buddhists call it setting the wheel of the dharma in motion.

title: The Four Noble Truths
description: Suffering (dukkha) marks the cycle of rebirth; its origin is craving; its cessation is nirvana; the path to its end is the Eightfold Path.

facts.text: The Four Noble Truths: suffering (dukkha) is a feature of the cycle of rebirth (samsara); its origin is craving (tanha); its cessation is nirvana; the path to its end is the Eightfold Path.
Dukkha, usually translated "suffering", also carries the sense of uneasiness or dissatisfaction, arising from a world that keeps changing.

title: The middle way
description: In his first sermon the Buddha described a middle way between self-indulgence and self-mortification, rejecting both extremes as fruitless.

facts.text: In his first sermon the Buddha described a middle way between the extremes of self-indulgence and self-mortification, rejecting both as fruitless.

title: The Eightfold Path and meditation
description: Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration, grouped into wisdom, ethics and concentration; meditation includes samatha and vipassana.

facts.text: The Eightfold Path is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration.

Buddhist tradition groups the path into three trainings: wisdom (right view and intention), ethics (right speech, action and livelihood) and concentration (right effort, mindfulness and concentration).
Buddhists practice samatha (calming) and vipassana (insight) meditation, learning to observe thoughts and feelings with detachment.

title: Impermanence and no self
description: Buddhist teaching names three characteristics of existence (impermanence, suffering, no-self); a person is five constantly changing factors with no permanent soul.

facts.text: Buddhist teaching names three characteristics of all existence: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha) and no-self (anatta).
Anatta is the teaching that there is in humans no permanent, underlying substance that can be called the soul; a person is made of five constantly changing factors (skandhas).

title: Nirvana
description: Nirvana, literally "blowing out", is the extinction of desire, hatred and ignorance and finally of suffering and rebirth; it is a state, not a place, reached in life and completed at death.

facts.text: Nirvana literally means "blowing out" or "becoming extinguished", as a flame is blown out.
Nirvana is the extinction of desire, hatred and ignorance and, ultimately, of suffering and rebirth; it is not regarded as a place but as an absence, above all of suffering.
Buddhists distinguish nirvana reached in life from final nirvana at death, when the causes of future existence are extinguished; the Buddha entered it at his death, never to be born again.

title: The Three Jewels
description: The Buddha, the dharma and the sangha; saying the refuge formula is how one becomes a Buddhist.

facts.text: The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the dharma (the teaching) and the sangha (the community).
One becomes a Buddhist by saying the refuge formula: "I go to the Buddha for refuge, I go to the Doctrine for refuge, I go to the Order for refuge."

title: Monastics and laypeople
description: The sangha has four groups (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen); the first monks were the five ascetics and an order of nuns followed; monastics depend on lay support, and givers gain merit.

facts.text: The sangha is traditionally made up of four groups: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.
The five ascetics of the first sermon became the first monks; at the request of his stepmother Mahaprajapati and other women, the Buddha also established an order of nuns.
The monastic order depends on the lay community for economic support, from alms to gifts of money and property.

In Thailand, monks traditionally walk barefoot before dawn to collect alms; the rules bar them from farming and they eat what is offered in their bowls; the monk blesses the food, and the giver gains merit.

title: Vesak
description: Vesak marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death on the full-moon day of Vesakha (April to June); laypeople make offerings and merit.

facts.text: Vesak commemorates the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha on the full-moon day of the month Vesakha, which falls in April, May or June.
At Vesak lay Buddhists offer flowers or light incense at temples and make merit through good deeds.

title: Theravada
description: The "Way of the Elders", predominant in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, with the Pali canon as scripture and the arhat as its ideal.

facts.text: Theravada, the "Way of the Elders", predominates in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos and recognizes the Pali canon as its scripture.
Theravada's ideal is the arhat, a perfected saint who reaches enlightenment through their own effort; traditionally the path runs through monastic life.

title: Mahayana and the bodhisattva
description: The "Greater Vehicle" arose around the beginning of the Common Era; predominant in East Asia; its bodhisattva delays nirvana to help all beings, and anyone can take that path.

facts.text: Mahayana, the "Greater Vehicle", arose within Indian Buddhism around the beginning of the Common Era and predominates in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
The Mahayana ideal is the bodhisattva, who vows to reach enlightenment but delays entering nirvana to help all other beings reach liberation; Mahayana teaches that anyone can become a bodhisattva.

title: Vajrayana
description: The "Thunderbolt" or "Diamond Vehicle", a later development within Mahayana, notably in Tibet, using mantras and mandalas.

facts.text: Vajrayana, the "Thunderbolt" or "Diamond Vehicle", is a later development within Mahayana, from India and neighboring lands, notably Tibet; it uses mantras to keep the mind from straying and mandalas, representations of the universe, as aids to meditation.

title: Guru Nanak's message
description: Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) returned from a river declaring "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim", taught devotion to one God's Name, honest work and sharing, and gathered the first Sikhs at Kartarpur.

facts.text: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, and died in 1539.
According to Sikh tradition, when he was about 30 Nanak disappeared while bathing in a river and after three days returned declaring, "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim."
Sikhism is monotheistic; Guru Nanak taught remembering God's Name, earning an honest living and sharing with others.
After years of travel, Nanak settled at Kartarpur, where the first Sikh community took shape.
The Punjabi word sikh means "learner".

title: The ten Gurus
description: From Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh (1469 to 1708), each Guru named a successor; Sikhs believe one spirit dwelt in all ten.

facts.text: Guru Nanak named his successor, Guru Angad, before his death in 1539, beginning a line of ten human Gurus that ended with Guru Gobind Singh in 1708.
Sikhs believe all 10 human Gurus were inhabited by a single spirit.

title: The langar and equality
description: The langar serves free vegetarian food to all, seated in one straight line, and began as a protest against caste.

facts.text: The langar, the communal kitchen of a gurdwara, serves vegetarian food to all, whatever their background, as an expression of the Sikh principle of equality.
In the langar everyone sits in a straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to show inferiority; the langar began as a protest against the caste system.

title: The Guru Granth Sahib
description: Compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 with hymns of Gurus and of Hindu and Muslim saints, the scripture became the Guru after Guru Gobind Singh's death in 1708.

facts.text: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, compiled the first version of the Adi Granth ("First Book") at Amritsar in 1604, with his own hymns, those of earlier Gurus, and songs of Hindu and Muslim saints, notably Kabir.
The Adi Granth's printed edition runs to 1,430 pages, with hymns arranged by the ragas, the musical modes in which they are sung.

Guru Gobind Singh declared the end of the line of personal Gurus; after his death in 1708 the scripture took the Guru's place as the Guru Granth Sahib, and worldly authority passed to the community (Panth).

title: The gurdwara
description: The "doorway to the Guru", where the scripture rests under a canopy, is opened each morning and put away at night, and worship ends at the langar.

facts.text: Gurdwara means "doorway to the Guru"; inside, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a cot under a canopy.
In gurdwaras the scripture is ritually opened in the morning and wrapped and put away for the night.
Gurdwara services feature scripture recitation and hymns sung with instruments; gurdwaras are open to all, and most have a langar, where the meal follows the hymns.

title: The Khalsa
description: Guru Gobind Singh, Guru since his father's execution in 1675, founded the Khalsa, a casteless order, on Baisakhi Day 1699, with amrit initiation and the names Singh and Kaur.

facts.text: Gobind Singh became the tenth Guru at nine, in 1675, after his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.
On Baisakhi Day in 1699, at Anandpur in Punjab, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, a casteless order of Sikhs committed to courage and their faith.
Khalsa initiation uses amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword (khanda).
Khalsa men take the name Singh ("lion") and women Kaur ("princess"), and members pledge to give up tobacco, alcohol and certain meats.

title: The Five Ks
description: Kesh, kara, kangha, kirpan and kachera: articles of faith worn by initiated Khalsa Sikhs, each with a meaning.

facts.text: Initiated Khalsa Sikhs wear the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair: belonging), kara (steel bracelet: self-restraint), kangha (comb: cleanliness), kirpan (sword: self-respect, readiness to face challenges), kachera (undergarment: moral restraint).

title: Buddhists and Sikhs today
description: About 4 percent of the world was Buddhist in 2020; Sikhs number about 25 million, most in India's Punjab state.

facts.text: Sikhism has about 25 million followers worldwide, most of them in the Indian state of Punjab.

title: Chinese ancestor veneration
description: Chinese families have honored ancestors since the Neolithic, with tablets on the home altar and offerings; many believe ancestors and the living help each other.

facts.text: Ancestor worship in China was deeply rooted and extensively developed by the Late Neolithic Period.
In China it was traditionally the head of a household's responsibility to see that offerings to the family's dead were constantly renewed.
On the Chinese home altar, wooden tablets carry each ancestor's name with birth and death dates, and incense is offered there morning and evening.
Ancestral spirits are believed to have the power to influence the lives of the living, and offerings seek to avoid misfortune and ensure good fortune.

title: Qingming, Tomb Sweeping Day
description: Qingming ('Clear and Bright'), in early April, is when Chinese families sweep ancestral tombs and leave offerings.

facts.text: Qingming, 'Clear and Bright', sometimes called Tomb Sweeping Day, falls on the 15th day after the spring equinox, generally in early April.
At Qingming families clean their ancestors' tombs and leave offerings, burning incense, spirit money and paper models of valuable goods.

title: Li: Confucian ritual and its rites
description: Li, ritual propriety, asks people to play every role properly, from state sacrifices at the Confucian temple to Taipei's ceremony on Confucius's birthday.

facts.text: Confucius traditionally lived from 551 to 479 BCE.
In Confucian teaching, li covers ritual, etiquette and social conventions, and expresses a willingness to play all of one's ritual roles.
The Analects urge not to look, listen, speak or move except in accordance with the rites.
Before 1911, China's imperial state rituals included sacrifices at the Confucian temple.
Each September 28 the Taipei Confucius Temple holds a commemoration ceremony for Confucius's birthday, with student ritual musicians.
Taiwan celebrates September 28, Confucius's birthday, as Teachers' Day.
The Taipei ceremony has three sections: welcoming Confucius's spirit, paying respects, and escorting the spirit away.

title: Filial piety (xiao)
description: Filial piety means serving parents properly in life and burying and sacrificing to them after death; ancestral sacrifice shows reverence and asks for help.

facts.text: Confucian filial piety (xiao) means serving one's parents with proper ritual while they live, then burying them and sacrificing to them properly after death.
Ancestral sacrifice showed reverence for ancestors and asked their spirits to help and protect the living.

title: Is Confucianism a religion?
description: Scholars once held that Confucianism was not really a religion; many now see its religious side, often as a 'diffused' religion lived in family and state.

facts.text: For most of the 20th century the predominant view was that Confucianism was not 'really' a religion, at least not like the more familiar Western traditions.
Most North American scholars of Confucianism today take its religious dimensions as evident, though the wider field still disagrees.
Following C. K. Yang, Joseph Adler calls Confucianism a 'diffused' religion, practiced in family, community and state rather than in a separate institution run by clergy.

title: Celestial Masters and Daoist priests
description: Daoists date their organized religion to a revelation traditionally dated 142 CE; daoshi priests of the Celestial Masters marry, while Quanzhen monks and nuns are celibate.

facts.text: By tradition, in 142 CE Laozi, worshipped as Lord Lao, appeared to Zhang Daoling and founded the Way of the Celestial Masters.
The main officiant of Daoist ritual is the daoshi, 'Daoist master', a role typically passed down within families.
Celestial Masters priests marry and live with their families, while Quanzhen is a celibate monastic order of monks and nuns, found mainly in northern China.
Beijing's White Cloud Abbey (Baiyun Guan), a Quanzhen temple, is the seat of the China Daoist Association.

title: The Daoist Offering (jiao)
description: The jiao renews a community's bond with its gods: priests inside the temple, a festival with the god's statue outside.

facts.text: The Daoist Offering ritual (jiao) renews the bond between a community and its gods; the Merit ritual (gongde) is a funeral rite.
A jiao usually lasts one to ten days; while priests perform it in the temple, a street festival carries the local god's statue through the neighborhood.

title: Daoist aims: long life and the Dao
description: Long life and immortality run through Daoist writing; liberation is pictured as union with the Dao, and immortals are people who went beyond ordinary limits.

facts.text: 'Long life' and 'immortality' are among the most recurrent terms in Daoist literature, and liberation is often pictured as union with the Dao.
Daoist immortals are said to be people who went beyond the limits of ordinary human existence, usually by means of their practices.
Quanzhen monks practice meditation and Internal Alchemy (neidan), often described as conceiving and bringing forth an immortal embryo within the body.

title: Buddhism arrives in China
description: Buddhism came to China with foreign merchants in the late Han; translators borrowed Chinese words, and monks adapted to a family-centered culture.

facts.text: Buddhism began to enter China as a religion of foreign merchants in the later years of the Han dynasty.
Early translators rendered 'sutra' as jing, the word already used for the Confucian and Daoist classics.
In China celibate monks and nuns seemed to some to threaten family values; monastics used kinship terms, and monks and lay donors held rituals to comfort the ancestors.

title: Chan (Zen) and Pure Land
description: Chan ('Meditation', Zen in Japanese) claims a transmission outside the scriptures; Pure Land devotees call on Amitabha Buddha for rebirth in his Pure Land.

facts.text: Chan, 'Meditation', from the Sanskrit dhyana, is known in Japanese as Zen.
Chan describes itself as 'a special transmission outside the scriptures', pointing directly to the human mind.
Pure Land devotees call on the name of Amitabha Buddha, hoping to be reborn in his Western Paradise, the Pure Land.

title: The three teachings (sanjiao)
description: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism came to be seen as three teachings in one sky, which is why people could honor all three.

facts.text: Sanjiao, the 'three teachings', are Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism.
The 6th-century scholar Li Shiqian wrote: 'Buddhism is the sun, Daoism the moon, and Confucianism the five planets.'

title: Kami
description: Shinto is 'the way of the kami': the sacred life-force of nature, ancestors and revered people; mountains such as Fuji can be kami themselves.

facts.text: The word Shinto literally means 'the way of the kami'.
The Association of Shinto Shrines describes kami as the divine energy or life-force of the natural world, with kami of rain, wind, mountains, sea and thunder.
Kami include ancestors, and people who gave great service to state or society may be enshrined and revered as kami.
The Association of Shinto Shrines says Shinto has no founder, no dogma and no doctrine.
Sacred mountains such as Mount Fuji are regarded as kami themselves and as dwelling places of kami.
Almost every shrine has a sacred forest, sometimes a single tree, and especially sacred trees are marked with a straw shimenawa rope.

title: The shrine and its torii
description: A jinja is the seat of kami; its torii marks the border between sacred space and the everyday world.

facts.text: A shrine (jinja) is the seat of one or more kami, and the place where the kami is present is especially sacred; often visitors may not enter it, or even see it.
A torii marks a shrine's entrance, the border between its sacred space and the everyday world, and many people bow slightly before passing through.
Every 20 years the main sanctuaries of Ise Jingu are rebuilt and the kami is moved to the new buildings.

title: Purity in Shinto
description: Purity is central in Shinto: visitors rinse at the font, shrines hold Oharae twice a year, and death is a source of ritual impurity.

facts.text: Purity is very important in Shinto, and most shrines have a water font where visitors rinse their hands and mouth before paying respects.
At the ends of June and December many shrines hold Oharae ceremonies to remove impurities built up over the previous six months.
In Shinto myth, Amaterasu, the most revered kami, was born when her father Izanagi cleansed himself after returning from the land of the dead.
Funerals are not normally held at shrines, because death is regarded as a source of ritual impurity.

title: Matsuri and shrine rites of passage
description: Matsuri thank the kami and carry them through the neighborhood; shrines also mark a child's first visit and Shichigosan.

facts.text: Matsuri offer gratitude to the kami and pray for the community's happiness, health and prosperity.
At many matsuri the kami is moved into a portable shrine, a mikoshi, and carried through the neighborhood.
The Niinamesai in November gives thanks for the rice harvest, and the day is now a national holiday, Labor Thanksgiving Day.
Babies are often brought to a shrine about a month after birth (hatsumiyamairi), and young children at Shichigosan, 'seven-five-three'.

title: Shinto and Buddhism in one life
description: Kami and buddhas were combined for about a thousand years until 1868; today most funerals are Buddhist and many Buddhists honor kami.

facts.text: By the late 8th century kami were thought to be avatars of buddhas, and this combined Shinto-Buddhist practice lasted until the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
A Japan Consumers' Association survey found about 90% of Japanese funerals were Buddhist.
In Pew's 2023 survey, 44% of Japanese Buddhists said they pray or offer respects to kami.

title: Threads many Native traditions share
description: Many Native American traditions tie religion to particular places, oral knowledge and relationships with other beings, while each nation's ways remain its own.

facts.text: Britannica describes religion in these traditions as the relationship between living humans and other persons or beings, however they are conceived.
Traditional knowledge, passed on orally across generations, keeps the memory of a place's visible and invisible inhabitants.

title: Sacred places of particular nations
description: The Diné homeland lies within four sacred mountains; more than two dozen tribes hold Bear Lodge (Devils Tower) sacred, each with its own histories.

facts.text: Four sacred mountains surround Dinétah, the Diné (Navajo) homeland: Blanca Peak (east), Mount Taylor (south), the San Francisco Peaks (west) and Hesperus Mountain (north).
The four mountains are sites of many events in Diné sacred stories and can be seen as forming a hogan, a Diné dwelling, that holds the Diné universe.
More than two dozen tribes, including the Arapaho, Crow, Cheyenne, Shoshone and Lakota, are associated with Devils Tower in Wyoming, which many call Bear Lodge.
Most tribes that lived in or near the Black Hills have their own oral histories of how the Tower was created.
Because June is a culturally significant time when many ceremonies occur, the park asks climbers to voluntarily stay off the Tower in June.

title: Sacred ways belong to their nation
description: Some sacred knowledge is restricted to those instructed and initiated; US law since 1978 protects Native peoples' right to practice their traditional religions.

facts.text: Access to some sacred knowledge is restricted, and some knowledge is considered so powerful that instruction and initiation are required.
The American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 made it US policy to protect Native peoples' right to believe, express and exercise their traditional religions, including access to sacred sites.

title: The Dreaming
description: The Dreaming, an English name for concepts like Jukurrpa and Tjukurpa, tells of Ancestral Beings who made the land and its law; it was, and is, 'everywhen'.

facts.text: 'The Dreaming' is an English translation of a First Nations concept with different names in different languages, such as Jukurrpa in Warlpiri.
Dreaming stories tell of Ancestral Beings who created animals, plants and land formations as they moved through the land, and who set out rules for living.
Older writing also called it the 'dream-time'.
The anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner said the Dreaming cannot be fixed in time: it 'was, and is, everywhen'.
Common Ground, a First Nations-led organization, says the Dreaming is not a religion and the Ancestral Beings are not gods.

title: Tjukurpa at Uluru
description: Anangu call it Tjukurpa: the religious philosophy and law linking them to land and ancestors, memorised and passed on; under it, climbing Uluru was not generally permitted.

facts.text: Anangu describe Tjukurpa as the religious philosophy linking them to the environment and their ancestors, and as their traditional law.
Tjukurpa is not written down: it is memorised and passed on to the right people, like an inheritance.
Anangu say that, like religions elsewhere in the world, Tjukurpa provides answers to many important questions.
Uluru is sacred to Anangu, and under Tjukurpa climbing it was not generally permitted.

title: Country
description: Country means the lands, waters and skies First Nations people are tied to by ancestry; there are hundreds, each with its own Law, and Country is spoken of as alive.

facts.text: First Nations people use Country for the lands, waters and skies they are connected to through ancestral ties; there are hundreds of Countries, each with its own culture, language and Law.
Country is spoken of like a person, as alive, and bound to its people by relationship and reciprocity: 'We are Country and Country is us.'

title: Olorun and the orisha
description: In Yoruba religion the Creator Olorun oversees some 400 orisha: primordial divinities, deified ancestors and forces of nature, to whom devotees turn.

facts.text: The Yoruba live mainly in southwestern Nigeria, with smaller groups in Benin and northern Togo.
Many Yoruba are now Christians or Muslims, but aspects of the traditional religion survive.
In Yoruba religion the Almighty Creator, Olorun, oversees the orisha; devotion to the orisha is active and widespread, but Olorun has neither priests nor cult groups.
Traditional Yoruba religion includes some 400 lesser gods and spirits, most with their own cults and priests.
Orisha fall into three overlapping kinds: primordial divinities, deified ancestors such as kings and city founders, and personified forces of nature.
Shango is both a deified ancestor, an early king of Oyo, and a natural force of fire and lightning.
Devotees turn to particular orisha for particular occupations, skills and problems.

title: Egungun: the ancestors return
description: At yearly festivals Egungun masqueraders, fully covered, become returned ancestors who bring blessings to the community.

facts.text: Egungun masquerades, often performed at yearly festivals, honor the ancestors and seek blessings for the community.
An Egungun costume, with gloves, foot covers and a mesh face screen, covers the performer and turns the wearer into a returned Yoruba ancestor.

title: Ifa divination
description: Ifa priests (babalawo) read signs with palm nuts and a chain, linking them to 256 odu of chanted verses, for important decisions.

facts.text: The Yoruba regard Ifa, also called Orunmila, as the deity of wisdom and intellectual development.
Ifa divination relies not on anyone's oracular powers but on signs read by a priest, the babalawo, using sacred palm nuts and a divination chain.
Ifa's literary corpus has 256 parts, the odu, each with many verses (about 800 per odu) that the priests chant.
Ifa is consulted whenever an important individual or collective decision has to be made, and its knowledge is passed on among Ifa priests.

title: Spirits in mountains, rivers and trees
description: Across East Asia, about half of adults or more in Taiwan, Japan and Vietnam say mountains, rivers or trees have their own spirits.

facts.text: In Pew's 2023 survey, about half of adults or more in Taiwan, Japan and Vietnam said mountains, rivers or trees have their own spirits.

title: How the Baha'i Faith began
description: The Baha'i Faith grew out of the Bab's movement, founded in Shiraz in 1844; Baha'u'llah declared his mission in 1863 and died in exile in 1892.

facts.text: The Baha'i Faith grew out of the Babi faith, founded in 1844 in Shiraz, Iran, by Mirza Ali Mohammad, known as the Bab.
Baha'u'llah was born in Tehran in 1817; in 1852, during the persecution of the Babis, he was thrown into a Tehran dungeon.
In 1863 Baha'u'llah declared to his fellow Babis that he was the messenger of God foretold by the Bab; exiled in Ottoman lands, he died near Akka in 1892.

title: The three onenesses
description: Baha'is sum up their teaching as the oneness of God, of religion and of humanity, and believe God has sent a series of Messengers in a progressive revelation.

facts.text: Baha'is sum up their teaching as the oneness of God, the oneness of religion and the oneness of humanity.
Baha'is believe God has sent a series of Messengers (Abraham, Krishna, Zoroaster, Moses, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Bab and Baha'u'llah), each suited to humanity's stage of growth.

title: A Baha'i community without clergy
description: The Baha'i Faith has no priesthood and is governed by the elected Universal House of Justice; its Houses of Worship, like the Lotus Temple, are open to all.

facts.text: The Baha'i Faith has no priesthood; its supreme governing body is the elected Universal House of Justice.
Baha'i Houses of Worship are open to people of all faiths or none.
The Baha'i House of Worship in New Delhi, the Lotus Temple, opened in December 1986; its 27 white marble 'petals', in clusters of three, form nine sides.

title: Vodou, Santería and Candomblé: roots
description: Vodou in Haiti, Santería in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil grew from West African traditions among enslaved Africans and their descendants, blended with Catholic elements.

facts.text: Vodou, an Afro-Haitian religion blending West African Vodun and Roman Catholicism, took shape in colonial Saint-Domingue (Haiti) among enslaved Dahomean, Kongo, Yoruba and other peoples.
The word Vodou means 'spirit' or 'deity' in the Fon language of the kingdom of Dahomey, now Benin.
Santería developed in Cuba from the religion of Yoruba people enslaved there in great numbers in the early 19th century; many practitioners call it Lukumí or Regla de Ocha.
Candomblé, strongest in the Brazilian state of Bahia, was created by enslaved Africans and their descendants and blends African beliefs with Catholic elements.
Most Candomblé devotees are women, and some terreiros (ritual communities) have long consecrated only women as their supreme leaders.
From the Cuban Revolution of 1959 into the 21st century, nearly one million Cubans left the island, bringing orisha religion to cities such as Miami and New York.

title: Spirits, orishas and saints
description: Vodouists honor the lwa beneath a creator God; Santería and Candomblé devotees linked the orishas with Catholic saints, often to keep worshipping when they could not do so openly.

facts.text: In Vodou, God is the 'great master' who leaves earthly matters to the lwa, spirits honored in temples led by priestesses (manbo) and priests (oungan).
The name Santería comes from correspondences some devotees made between the Yoruba orishas and the saints (santos) of Roman Catholic piety.
Unable to practice Candomblé openly, devotees outwardly equated the orixás with Catholic saints.

title: How Rastafari began
description: Rastafari began in 1930s Jamaica after Haile Selassie I, formerly Ras Tafari, was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1930; many Rastas regard him as the messiah.

facts.text: Rastafari began in Jamaica in the 1930s, after Haile Selassie I was crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1930; it takes its name from his precoronation name, Ras Tafari.
Many Rastas regard Haile Selassie I as the messiah, the Second Coming of Christ, who came to redeem Black people.

title: Babylon and Zion
description: Rastas see people of African descent as exiles in Babylon, tested by Jah, and Ethiopia (Zion) as the home of all Africans.

facts.text: Rastas see people of African descent as exiles in 'Babylon', tested by Jah (God) through slavery and economic injustice, and Ethiopia, called Zion, as the ultimate home of all Africans.

title: Rastafari in practice
description: Rastafari has no central church; its practices include dreadlocks, an ital diet, ganja for meditation and all-night drumming ceremonies.

facts.text: Rasta practices include wearing dreadlocks, eating an 'ital' (natural, vegetarian) diet, smoking ganja for meditation, and all-night drumming ceremonies.
No formal central church emerged in Rastafari; its different groups share core beliefs.

title: America's religious freedom laws
description: Virginia's 1786 statute, the First Amendment's Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses (1791) and Article VI's ban on religious tests set out religious freedom in American law.

facts.text: Virginia enacted its Statute for Religious Freedom on January 16, 1786: no one could be compelled to support any religious worship or suffer for their religious opinions or belief.
Thomas Jefferson wrote the Virginia statute, James Madison guided it to passage while Jefferson was abroad, and Jefferson had his authorship listed on his tombstone.
The First Amendment, ratified in 1791, begins: 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'.
The First Amendment's two religion clauses are the Establishment Clause, which bars government establishment of religion, and the Free Exercise Clause, which protects religious practice.
Article VI of the Constitution says 'no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States'.

title: The 'wall of separation'
description: Jefferson's 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists gave America the phrase 'a wall of separation between Church & State'.

facts.text: The Danbury Baptist Association of Connecticut wrote to President Jefferson complaining of religious oppression by their state government and supporting freedom of conscience.
In his letter of January 1, 1802, Jefferson wrote that religion 'lies solely between Man & his God' and that the First Amendment built 'a wall of separation between Church & State'.
In 1976 Census Bureau director Vincent Barabba said a mandatory census question on religion would appear to infringe upon the traditional separation of church and state.

title: The Great Awakening
description: A revival in the British American colonies from about 1720 to the 1740s, with Whitefield's preaching tours, Edwards's theology and the call to a 'new birth'.

facts.text: The Great Awakening was a religious revival in the British American colonies mainly between about 1720 and the 1740s.
In 1739 and 1740 George Whitefield, an Anglican priest, preached up and down the colonies to vast crowds; Jonathan Edwards was the revival's great thinker and defender.
Revival preachers stressed the unmerited grace of God and the 'new birth' in Jesus Christ.

title: The Second Great Awakening
description: A Protestant revival from about 1795 to 1835 whose camp meetings, like Cane Ridge in 1801, grew the Methodist and Baptist churches and stirred reforms.

facts.text: The Second Great Awakening was a Protestant revival in the United States from about 1795 to 1835; many churches grew, particularly Methodist and Baptist churches.
At camp meetings, families drove their wagons to the meeting ground, pitched tents and stayed for several days; the Kentucky revivals stirred intense emotion.
Barton Stone organized the Cane Ridge revival near Lexington, Kentucky, in the summer of 1801.
The revivals helped make the teachings of the Baptists and Methodists accessible to a wider cross section of people.
The Second Great Awakening stimulated moral and philanthropic reforms, including temperance and the emancipation of women.

title: How the Latter-day Saints began
description: Joseph Smith reported a vision in 1820 and golden plates shown by the angel Moroni; he published the Book of Mormon and organized a church in 1830.

facts.text: Joseph Smith, who grew up in Palmyra, New York, reported that in 1820, at age 14, God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him.
Smith reported that in 1823 an angel named Moroni told him of golden plates; he published the Book of Mormon in March 1830 and organized a church on April 6, 1830.
The Church teaches that Joseph Smith translated the plates 'by the gift and power of God' and that the Book of Mormon is another witness of Jesus Christ that supports the Bible.
Latter-day Saints hold to continuing revelation and emphasize temple worship and missionary work.

title: The trek to Utah
description: After moves to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo and Joseph Smith's killing in 1844, Brigham Young led the Saints to the Salt Lake Valley, a region they called Deseret.

facts.text: Latter-day Saints moved from New York to Ohio, then Missouri, then Illinois, where they built the city of Nauvoo.
On June 27, 1844, Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum were shot by a mob while held in jail at Carthage, Illinois.
Brigham Young led a 1,100-mile migration to Utah in 1846 and 1847; the first company entered the Salt Lake Valley in July 1847.
In the Book of Mormon, 'deseret' means honeybee; settlers called their region Deseret, and the beehive became Utah's symbol of industry.

title: The Seventh-day Adventists
description: After William Miller's predictions of the Second Coming failed in 1844, a small group kept a Saturday Sabbath and organized the Seventh-day Adventist Church in 1863.

facts.text: William Miller predicted Christ's Second Coming in 1843 and then 1844; when it did not come, most followers left, and the letdown became known as the Great Disappointment.
Some Adventists became convinced that Saturday, not Sunday, is the Sabbath God commanded; the Seventh-day Adventist Church was organized at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1863.
Ellen G. White (1827 to 1915), who reported visions, had a dominant influence on the Seventh-day Adventist Church for many years.

title: Jehovah's Witnesses
description: Jehovah's Witnesses grew from Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students of the 1870s, took their name in 1931 and are known for door-to-door witnessing.

facts.text: Charles Taze Russell founded a Bible Students movement in Pittsburgh in 1872; in 1931 it took the name Jehovah's Witnesses, from the conviction that Jehovah is God's name.
Witnesses see Jesus as God's agent rather than part of a Trinity, expect a coming kingdom on earth, and are known for door-to-door preaching called witnessing.

title: Pentecostalism
description: Pentecostalism spread from the 1906 Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles, led by William J. Seymour, and emphasizes baptism with the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues.

facts.text: Pentecostalism spread nationally and internationally from the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles, begun in 1906 and led by William J. Seymour, an African American minister who welcomed worshipers of every race.
Pentecostals emphasize baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually accompanied by speaking in tongues, as at the Pentecost described in Acts.

title: Independent Black churches
description: Black Methodists left a Philadelphia church in 1787; Richard Allen became bishop of the AME Church in 1816, and Black churches became hubs of community life.

facts.text: In 1787 Black worshippers withdrew from St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia because of restrictions in seating; Richard Allen, formerly enslaved, became their leader.
In 1816 Richard Allen was consecrated bishop of the newly organized African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church, the first African American denomination organized in the United States.
Churches founded by free African American Christians became the hub of Black economic, social and intellectual life in many areas.
In 1819 Richard Allen authorized Jarena Lee to preach, the first woman licensed by the AME Church; he had first told her its rules did not call for women preachers.

title: The Nation of Islam and after
description: The Nation of Islam, founded in Detroit in 1930, preached self-help and Black enterprise; after 1975 Warith Deen Mohammed led most members toward orthodox Islam.

facts.text: Wallace D. Fard founded the Nation of Islam in Detroit in 1930; under Elijah Muhammad, its leader from 1934, it preached racial unity, self-help and Black-owned businesses.
Nation of Islam members were encouraged to replace their surnames with Muslim names or an 'X', marking identities lost in slavery.
After Elijah Muhammad died in 1975, his son Warith Deen Mohammed moved followers toward orthodox Islam, and most joined the wider Muslim community.

title: Immigration since 1965
description: The 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act ended national-origin limits; new Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and other communities followed, while most immigrants stayed Christian.

facts.text: The Immigration and Nationality Act, signed on October 3, 1965, ended America's long policy of limiting immigration by national origin and opened new opportunities for immigrants from Asia.

Since the 1965 act, Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Zoroastrians and new communities of Jews and Catholics have arrived, and mosques, temples and gurdwaras stand in virtually every major US city.
Christians were 68% of new legal immigrants in 1992 and 61% in 2012, while the share belonging to religious minorities rose from about one in five (19%) to one in four (25%).

title: Americans' faith today
description: Pew's 2023 to 2024 Religious Landscape Study found about 62% of US adults Christian, 29% unaffiliated and 7% of other faiths, with belief in God far wider than affiliation.

facts.text: Pew's 2023 to 2024 Religious Landscape Study of 36,908 US adults found 62% Christian, 29% religiously unaffiliated and 7% of other religions, including Jews, Muslims, Buddhists and Hindus.
After years of decline, the share of Americans who identify as Christian shows signs of leveling off.
In the same study, 83% of US adults said they believe in God or a universal spirit.

title: How new faiths take root
description: New faiths often begin with a founder's revelation or a revival and grow out of older traditions, as the Latter-day Saints did from early 19th-century American revivalism.

facts.text: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints emerged from the revivalist Christian movements of early 19th-century America.

title: Halakhah, Jewish law
description: Halakhah, 'the Way', is Jewish law for observance and daily life, built through the Mishnah and Talmud and read differently by Jewish movements.

facts.text: Halakhah, Hebrew for 'the Way', is the body of Jewish law regulating religious observance and daily conduct, such as keeping the Sabbath.
Jews trace halakhah to the revelation at Sinai; it developed through the Mishnah, compiled in the early 3rd century CE, and the Talmud.
Orthodox and Conservative Judaism treat halakhah as binding, Conservative rabbis adapting some laws to modern conditions; Reform Judaism holds most of it not binding.

title: Canon law
description: Canon law is the law church authorities make for their churches; it binds members, not the state, though it shaped secular law.

facts.text: Canon law is law made by church authority to govern a church and its members, used in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches.
Canon 11 of the Catholic Code of Canon Law says merely ecclesiastical laws bind those baptized in or received into the Catholic Church.
Canon law does not bind the state, but it influenced secular law in areas such as marriage law and criminal procedure.

title: Sharia and fiqh
description: Sharia is the path Muslims believe God ordained; fiqh is the human work of understanding it, and most Muslim-majority states keep it mainly for family law.

facts.text: Sharia is, for Muslims, a divinely ordained path of conduct; scholars derive it from the Quran and the Sunnah, with consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas).
Sharia covers a Muslim's relationship with God, such as prayer and fasting, as well as dealings with neighbors and the state.
Fiqh, 'understanding', is the human science of working out sharia's precise terms, and schools of law hold a wide range of positions on almost every point.
From the 19th century most Muslim countries adopted Western-style criminal codes, keeping sharia mainly for family law such as marriage, divorce and inheritance.

title: Why a lunar year drifts
description: A purely lunar year of about 354 days is about 11 days short of the solar year, so Ramadan moves through the seasons.

facts.text: Twelve lunar months make a year of about 354 days, about 11 days shorter than the solar year of about 365 days that solar calendars follow.
The Islamic calendar is purely lunar, 12 months of 354 or 355 days with no leap months, so its months, including the ninth, Ramadan, move through all the seasons in about 32.5 years.

title: Lunisolar calendars
description: Hebrew and Hindu calendars count moons but add leap months so festivals such as Passover and Diwali stay in season.

facts.text: The Hebrew calendar is lunisolar: a leap month, First Adar, is added seven times in 19 years so the major festivals stay in season; Passover begins on 15 Nisan, in spring.
The Hindu calendar reconciles 12 lunar months with the solar year by adding extra months, and most major Hindu festivals shift each year against the Gregorian calendar.
Diwali centers on the new moon around the start of the lunar month Karttika, where Ashvina and Karttika meet, and falls in late October or November.

title: The Easter rule
description: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after March 21, between March 22 and April 25.

facts.text: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox, fixed by the Church at March 21, so it falls between March 22 and April 25.

title: Kosher and halal
description: Kosher and halal rules rest on scripture and God's command: permitted animals, forbidden pork, proper slaughter.

facts.text: Kosher law permits mammals that chew the cud and have cloven hooves and fish with fins and scales, so no pork or shellfish, and keeps meat and dairy strictly apart.
Kosher rules come from the Torah, in books such as Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and for observant Jews no motive is needed beyond God's command.
Halal means permitted by Islamic law and haram forbidden; pork, alcohol, blood and carrion are prohibited, and the slaughterer invokes God's name.
Whether a food is halal is judged from the Quran, the Hadith, analogy and scholarly consensus, the sources of Islamic law.

title: Food and not harming
description: Hindu, Jain and Buddhist food customs grow from not harming living beings, practiced with different strictness.

facts.text: The ideal of not harming sentient creatures, taught by Jains and Buddhists, was taken up in Hinduism and applied especially to the cow.
In a Pew survey of India published in 2021, 44% of Hindus and 92% of Jains said they were vegetarian, and most Hindus said a person who eats beef cannot be Hindu.
Jain teaching advises against root vegetables because pulling up the roots destroys the whole plant; 67% of Jains in Pew's India survey avoid them.
Buddhism's first precept is to refrain from taking life; early monks and nuns ate the alms they were given but not animals slaughtered specifically for them.
Vegetarian meals became the norm in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries, while in Theravada and Tibetan Buddhism vegetarianism is a personal choice.

title: Why Judaism and Islam avoid images of God
description: The Second Commandment and Islam's aniconism turn worship away from images toward words and pattern.

facts.text: Exodus 20:4 in the King James Version reads: 'Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above...'
The commandment's aim was idol worship rather than all art: the 3rd-century synagogue at Dura-Europos was painted with biblical scenes.
Muslims generally reject images of God and of the Prophet Muhammad, seeing them as a form of idolatry inconsistent with monotheism.
Islamic aniconism rests on the belief that God alone is the author of life; in mosques the arabesque is said to represent the infinite vastness of God.

title: The fight over icons
description: Byzantine iconoclasts attacked icons as idolatry; defenders held that honor passes to the person shown; icons returned in 843.

facts.text: From the 720s Byzantine emperors, beginning with Leo III, attacked the veneration of icons as idolatry, citing the Ten Commandments; in 843 Empress Theodora restored icons for good.
Defenders of icons stressed that images are symbols and created matter has dignity, and taught that honor shown to an icon passes to the holy person it shows.

title: Zakat, charity and dana
description: Zakat is an obligatory share that purifies; Christians hear Jesus in the needy; Buddhist dana builds merit.

facts.text: Zakat, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is one-fortieth (about 2.5 percent) of cash and savings above a minimum threshold, the nisab; those below it are exempt.
The Quran's ninth sura names zakat's recipients, including the poor and needy, people in debt and travelers in need.
The word zakat literally means 'purification', and Muslims believe paying it purifies the rest of their wealth.
In Matthew 25 (King James Version) the King says, 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat', and 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.'
Dana, Buddhist gift-giving such as food and robes for monks or gifts to temples, builds merit, which Buddhists believe improves karma and leads to a better rebirth.

title: Tzedakah
description: Tzedakah means justice or righteousness; Maimonides ranked helping someone stand on their own highest.

facts.text: The Hebrew word tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice or righteousness, so giving is treated as doing what is right rather than optional charity.

In his 12th-century code, the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides ranked highest a gift, loan or business partnership that helps the poor person stand on their own, then giving where neither side knows the other.

title: The langar
description: The Sikh langar serves everyone in one line, expressing selfless service and equality.

facts.text: A Sikh langar serves vegetarian food to all who come; everyone sits in a straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to show inferiority.
The langar embodies the Sikh principles of selfless service and equality.

title: Caste and India's constitution
description: Varna and jati ranked people by birth; India's 1950 constitution bans caste discrimination and abolishes untouchability.

facts.text: Ancient texts describe four varnas, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, an arrangement traced to a hymn preserved in the Rigveda.
Everyday caste ran on jatis, birth groups that traditionally married within themselves and were tied to hereditary occupations.
People assigned work seen as impure, such as handling dead animals, were treated as untouchable; many in these communities now prefer the name Dalit.
India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950; Article 15 bans discrimination based on caste, and Article 17 abolishes untouchability.

title: Challengers of caste
description: The Buddha, bhakti poets such as Ravidas, the Sikh langar, Hindu reformers and B. R. Ambedkar each challenged caste by birth.

facts.text: In the Vasala Sutta the Buddha teaches that no one is an outcast or a brahman by birth; by deeds one becomes either.
The bhakti poet Ravidas, born into a leatherworking caste considered untouchable, taught that all are made from the same clay by the same creator; about 40 of his poems are in the Sikh scripture.
Britannica notes that the Sikh langar originated as a protest against the caste system.
The Arya Samaj, a Hindu reform movement founded by Dayananda Sarasvati in 1875, opposed basing caste on birth rather than merit and rejected untouchability.
B. R. Ambedkar, born into a Dalit Mahar family, chaired the drafting committee of India's constitution.
In October 1956, in despair that untouchability persisted in Hindu doctrine, Ambedkar became a Buddhist at a ceremony in Nagpur with about 200,000 fellow Dalits.

title: Ahimsa
description: Ahimsa, not harming living things, is shared by Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism, most strictly by Jains.

facts.text: Ahimsa is the ethical principle of not causing harm to living things, shared by Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism.
In Jainism ahimsa is the standard by which all actions are judged, extending to insects, plants and microbes and even to thoughts; Hindus and Buddhists apply it less strictly.

title: Gandhi's satyagraha
description: Gandhi turned ahimsa into satyagraha, 'holding onto truth', nonviolent resistance to injustice.

facts.text: Gandhi grew up in Gujarat in a home with a strong tinge of Jainism and embraced ahimsa, vegetarianism and fasting for self-purification.
Satyagraha, 'holding onto truth', is Gandhi's nonviolent resistance to injustice, first conceived in 1906 against anti-Asian laws in South Africa's Transvaal.
Gandhi drew satyagraha from ahimsa, Hindu and biblical texts, and Tolstoy and Thoreau, and used it in campaigns such as the Salt March of 1930.

title: King's Christian nonviolence
description: Martin Luther King Jr. drew his motive from Christ and his method from Gandhi.

facts.text: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister who first met Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolence as a student at Crozer Theological Seminary.
King first used nonviolent direct action in the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 to 1956.
King wrote that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method', and grounded nonviolence in agape, redeeming good will for all.

title: Persecution in history
description: From Roman persecution of Christians to the 1492 expulsion and the Holocaust, persecution for faith is documented, and the UN still reports it.

facts.text: Diocletian began the last major Roman persecution of Christians in 303 CE; the Edict of Milan of 313 established religious toleration for Christianity.
On 31 March 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella gave Spain's Jews the choice of exile or baptism; Britannica puts those expelled at more than 160,000.
The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators, 1933 to 1945.
In 2022 UN human rights experts said arbitrary arrests of Baha'is in Iran and the destruction or confiscation of their property bore all the signs of a policy of systematic persecution.

title: Article 18
description: The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to change it.

facts.text: After the Second World War, the nations of the new United Nations vowed never again to allow atrocities like those of that conflict, and drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
On 10 December 1948, meeting in Paris, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights with eight abstentions and none against.
The Declaration's preamble says disregard and contempt for human rights 'have resulted in barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind'.
Article 18: 'Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion', including freedom to change religion or belief and to practice it alone or with others, in public or private.

title: The conflict thesis and its critics
description: Draper and White told science and religion as a war; most historians now see a far more complex history.

facts.text: The warfare story was spread by John William Draper's History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896).
The conflict model leans on Galileo's trial and Darwin's reception; most scholars of science and religion now see it as a shallow and partisan reading of the record.
From the late 1980s historians such as John Hedley Brooke (1991) studied science and religion in detailed historical context.

title: Galileo and Darwin reconsidered
description: Galileo was a believer condemned in 1633; Darwin's religious readers ranged from condemnation to support.

facts.text: In 1633 the Inquisition sentenced Galileo to life imprisonment for teaching that Earth moves around the Sun; he served it under house arrest until his death in 1642 and was not tortured or executed.
In his 1615 letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, Galileo quoted a churchman: the Holy Spirit's intention is to teach how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.
Letters to Darwin after On the Origin of Species (1859) ranged from complete condemnation to active support; clergyman Charles Kingsley's praise was added to the second edition.
Asa Gray, an American botanist and devout Presbyterian, defended natural selection and was one of Darwin's leading supporters.

title: Lemaitre, priest and cosmologist
description: A Belgian priest proposed the Big Bang's forerunner in 1927 and kept science and faith distinct.

facts.text: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian ordained a Catholic priest in 1923, proposed in 1927 the theory that grew into the Big Bang.
In 1958 Lemaitre called his model a scientific hypothesis entirely outside metaphysics or religion, and he objected when Pius XII suggested in 1951 that cosmology supported creation.

title: Ideas crossing between faiths
description: Religious ideas cross borders: King's 1959 trip to India shows nonviolence passing from one faith and country to another.

facts.text: In 1959 King made a five-week trip to India, meeting Gandhi's family, Indian activists and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.

title: America's separation of church and state
description: The First Amendment bars an established religion and protects free exercise; the Census Bureau cited church-state separation in 1976.

facts.text: The First Amendment says: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."
In 1976 the Census Bureau's director said a religion question on the mandatory census would appear to infringe upon the traditional separation of church and state.

title: France's laïcité
description: France's 1905 law guarantees freedom of conscience and recognizes, pays for and subsidizes no religion; religion is private and public schools stay free of conspicuous religious symbols.

facts.text: France's 1905 law says the Republic ensures freedom of conscience, and neither recognizes, pays for nor subsidizes any religion.
French laïcité treats religion as a private matter and keeps a secular public sphere.
A French law of 15 March 2004 bans public school students from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, such as Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and large crosses.

title: India's secularism
description: India's constitution protects religious freedom; 'secular' joined its preamble in 1976; its secularism balances equal respect for all religions with neutrality and allows religious personal law.

facts.text: India's constitution protected religious freedom and banned religious discrimination from the start; the word secular was added to its preamble in 1976.
Britannica describes Indian secularism as balancing Gandhi's sarva dharma sama bhava, the equality of all religions, with Nehru's neutrality toward religion.
In India, Muslims may follow Islamic law and Hindus Hindu law in family matters such as marriage and inheritance.

title: Atheism and its long history
description: Atheism denies belief in God or spiritual beings; India's ancient Lokayata school already rejected god, soul and afterlife.

facts.text: Britannica defines atheism as the critique and denial of metaphysical beliefs in God or spiritual beings; the word comes from the Greek atheos, "godless".
India's Lokayata school, also called Carvaka, rejected god, an immaterial soul and the afterlife, and accepted perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge.
No doctrinal works of the Lokayata school survive; only fragments remain.

title: Agnosticism
description: Huxley coined 'agnostic' in 1869; agnostics leave the question of God open rather than denying it.

facts.text: T. H. Huxley introduced the word agnosticism in 1869 at a meeting of the Metaphysical Society in London.
Huxley said the word came to him as the opposite of the "Gnostic" of Church history, who professed to know so much about things of which Huxley was ignorant.
Atheism denies that God exists, while agnosticism leaves the question open, finding it unanswered or unanswerable.

title: Secular humanism
description: Humanism is a nonreligious ethical life stance; many humanists are atheists or agnostics; Holyoake coined 'secularism' in 1851.

facts.text: Humanists International describes humanism as a democratic and ethical life stance affirming that human beings have the right and responsibility to give meaning and shape to their own lives.
Humanists International says many humanists are atheists and others agnostic, and that humanists do not believe in gods or an afterlife.
George Holyoake first used the word secularism in 1851, for a nonreligious civic and ethical philosophy.

title: The rise of American nones
description: The unaffiliated share of US adults grew from 16% (2007) to 29% (2023-24) and has recently plateaued.

facts.text: In Pew's Religious Landscape Studies, religiously unaffiliated Americans rose from 16% of adults in 2007 to 23% in 2014 and 29% in 2023-24.
The 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study surveyed 36,908 US adults.
Pew reports that the share of religiously unaffiliated Americans has plateaued in recent years after a long period of growth.
In the 2023-24 study, 19% of US adults were raised Christian and now say they are religiously unaffiliated.

title: Who the nones are
description: Most US nones say 'nothing in particular'; atheists and agnostics are minorities among them.

facts.text: In Pew's 2023 data, 17% of US religious nones identified as atheist, 20% as agnostic and 63% as "nothing in particular".

title: Believing without belonging
description: Most US nones believe in God or a higher power; many are spiritual; their reasons focus on questioning teachings and disliking institutions.

facts.text: Pew found that most US religious nones believe in God or some other higher power.
About half of US nones say spirituality is very important in their lives or think of themselves as spiritual.
Two-thirds of US nones say they question a lot of religious teachings or don't believe in God, and 47% cite disliking religious organizations as a very important reason.

title: The secularization thesis
description: Berger (1967) defined secularization and, like many sociologists, expected modernization to erode religion; Bruce still defends the thesis, and structural secularization happened in much of Europe.

facts.text: In The Sacred Canopy (1967), Peter Berger defined secularization as "the process by which sectors of society and culture are removed from the domination of religious institutions and symbols", as when education left church authority.
The early Berger saw secularization as an inevitable result of modernization and, like many sociologists of his time, saw little future for religion.
Sociologist Steve Bruce defended the secularization thesis in a 2011 book, tying religion's decline to modernization.
Most sociologists of religion agree that institutions separating from religion has happened in much of Europe, at least.

title: Berger's about-face
description: In 1999 Berger declared the world 'as furiously religious as it ever was', calling the secularized-world assumption false.

facts.text: In 1999 Berger wrote that "the assumption that we live in a secularized world is false" and that the world is "as furiously religious as it ever was".

title: Why the world's religious map changes
description: From 2010 to 2020 switching grew the unaffiliated, while youthful, higher-fertility religious populations grew fastest; religious numbers still rose.

facts.text: From 2010 to 2020 the Muslim share of the world rose 1.8 points to 25.6%, the Christian share fell 1.8 points to 28.8%, and the unaffiliated share rose nearly a point to 24.2%.
Religious switching, especially people raised Christian shedding their religious identity, explains much of the unaffiliated population's growth from 2010 to 2020.
Muslims grew fastest from 2010 to 2020, helped by their youthfulness, while the unaffiliated are older and have lower fertility than Christians, Muslims and Hindus.
From 2010 to 2020 the number of Muslims grew by 347 million and the number of Christians by 122 million.

title: Juergensmeyer's cosmic war
description: Juergensmeyer studies religious motives in violence: 'cosmic war' frames a conflict as good against evil, though he holds that violence has social, political and economic causes.

facts.text: Mark Juergensmeyer's Terror in the Mind of God draws on interviews to study violence among Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist groups.
Juergensmeyer uses "cosmic war" for the image of a broader conflict between good and evil, right and wrong, not just a fight fought for religious reasons.

Juergensmeyer says he does not believe religion causes violence, which happens for a complex variety of social, political and economic reasons; religion brings "a structure of justification and meaning".

title: Cavanaugh's myth of religious violence
description: Cavanaugh argues there is no timeless essence of religion, so 'religious violence' is a misleading category shaped by power.

facts.text: In The Myth of Religious Violence (2009), William Cavanaugh argues there is no transhistorical and transcultural essence of religion; what counts as religious or secular depends on configurations of power.
Cavanaugh argues that the idea of religion as non-rational and prone to violence is one of the foundational legitimating myths of Western society.

title: Mystics across traditions
description: Sufis, Kabbalists, Christian contemplatives like Teresa of Ávila and Zen practitioners each seek the sacred directly.

facts.text: Britannica defines Sufism as mystical Islamic belief and practice in which Muslims seek the truth of divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God.
Kabbalah is esoteric Jewish mysticism; its great book, the Zohar ("Book of Splendour"), appeared in medieval Spain and in some circles gained a sanctity rivaling the Torah's.
The Spanish Carmelite nun Teresa of Ávila described the soul's progress toward God through prayer in The Interior Castle.
Zen, a school of East Asian Buddhism named from the Sanskrit dhyana, "meditation", seeks awakening through meditation as "a special transmission outside the scriptures".

title: William James's marks of mysticism
description: James (1902) named ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity; the first two are enough to call a state mystical.

facts.text: In The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), William James named four marks of mystical states: ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity.
James held that ineffability and a noetic quality are enough to call a state mystical: it defies expression in words, yet feels like a state of knowledge.

title: One path or many?
description: Perennialists see a common core in mystical experience; constructivists like Katz argue each tradition shapes the experience itself.

facts.text: James saw in Hinduism, Sufism and Christian mysticism one tradition "hardly altered by differences of clime or creed", but admitted that on a wider view "the supposed unanimity largely disappears".
Perennialists such as Aldous Huxley (1945) hold that mystical doctrines transcend all cultures and religions.
In 1978 Steven Katz argued that there are no pure, unmediated experiences: a mystic's religious setting shapes, even over-determines, the experience itself.

title: 'New religious movement', not 'cult'
description: Every religion was new once; 'cult' went from a neutral term to a slur, so scholars prefer 'new religious movement' to avoid prejudging a group.

facts.text: Eileen Barker notes that all religions were new at their inception; early Christianity was a sect within the Judaic tradition, and early Methodism a sect within Christianity.

Church, sect, denomination and cult were once technical, non-judgmental terms in sociology; in popular speech today "cult" can suggest a dangerous pseudo-religion that exploits recruits with brainwashing.
Britannica calls "new religious movement" the generally accepted term for what is sometimes called, often pejoratively, a cult.
Barker argues that to discover whether a movement commits crimes or abuse, it must be defined independently of those traits; since the 1970s scholars have preferred "new religious movement".
Britannica notes that the concept of brainwashing peaked in the 1970s but has since lost credibility.

title: Judging any group by its actions
description: New movements differ widely, so each must be judged by what it believes and does at a given time and place.

facts.text: Barker writes that new religious movements differ in beliefs, practices, leadership, finances and potential for harm, and that no activity is typical of them and atypical of older religions.

Because new religious movements differ so much, Barker says each must be looked at according to what it believes and does at a particular time and place, without confusing the movement, its leaders and its members.
In 1988 Barker founded Inform, an educational charity giving information about minority religions that is as accurate and up to date as possible.

title: The 1893 Parliament of Religions
description: Chicago's 1893 Parliament began the modern interfaith movement, though Christians dominated and Native Americans were excluded.

facts.text: The World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago from 11 to 27 September 1893, in the building that became the Art Institute of Chicago.
The 1893 Parliament is regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement.
English-speaking Christians delivered 152 of the 194 papers at the 1893 Parliament, and Native Americans were excluded.
In his final address at the 1893 Parliament, the Hindu monk Vivekananda said every religion's banner would soon read "Help and not fight".

title: Nostra Aetate
description: The Catholic Church's 1965 declaration rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, esteems Muslims, decries antisemitism and urges dialogue.

facts.text: Nostra Aetate, proclaimed by Pope Paul VI on 28 October 1965, says the Catholic Church "rejects nothing that is true and holy" in other religions.
Nostra Aetate says the Church regards Muslims with esteem and decries hatred and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews.
The same declaration says the Church "ever must proclaim Christ", while urging dialogue and collaboration with followers of other religions.

title: Ground rules for dialogue
description: Swidler's Dialogue Decalogue: dialogue aims to learn; each partner describes their own faith; compare ideals with ideals and practice with practice.

facts.text: Leonard Swidler's Dialogue Decalogue holds that the essential purpose of dialogue is to learn.
Swidler's rules say each participant describes their own faith, and that ideals should be compared with ideals and practice with practice.

title: Where believers actually live
description: Most Muslims live in the Asia-Pacific region, and more Christians live in sub-Saharan Africa than in Europe.

facts.text: In 2020, about 59% of the world's Muslims lived in the Asia-Pacific region.
In 2020, 30.7% of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 22.3% in Europe.
